speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission I should like to table a copy, in each of the official languages, of the order in council passed yesterday amending the war claims regulations. Perhaps I might be permitted to say, by way of explanation, that it does two things. It changes priority for payment of claims so that small property claims under $2,500 can be paid as soon as they have been properly processed. Nearly all the personal claims, except those that are difficult to adjudicate, have already been paid, and the government is now satisfied there will be funds available to pay the small property claims, without jeopardizing any of the personal claims.
There is another section which extends the time for making a claim to September 30 of this year. I found on checking the other day that there were 15 or so of these claims that had come in too late. Some of them had come early in January, although the deadline was December 31. It seemed to be rather unfair, when some of these claims were for small amounts, and were really compassionate cases, that they should not have their claims adjudicated. I do not expect there will be any further extension. It is intended that this will be the final date for receiving these claims.

Resolution No. 78. Hon. members will find the vote at page 12 of the blue book, and the details commencing at page 152.
78. Departmental administration and payments to Canadian Commercial Corporation and other corporate agencies for services provided in connection with defence purchasing and production, $6,446,812.
Is it the minister's intention to make a statement reviewing the operations of this department?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes, it is. A good deal of information concerning our defence production program was made available during the recent debate on the estimates of the Department of National Defence. In addition, hon. members have been provided with an excellent white paper tabled by my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, as well as the annual report of the Department of Defence Production, which was tabled in March.
However, I believe that I might usefully say a few words about our major procurement programs in order to indicate the scope and nature of our industrial potential, and to outline the activity of the Department of Defence Production.
As nearly one-half of the purchases of defence equipment are made on behalf of the R.C.A.F., it is appropriate that I start with our aircraft program. Without going into detail on the program itself, I would like to make a few general comments regarding our development and production policy in the aircraft field.
Hon. members have stressed the viewpoint that we should make every effort to correlate our research and development activities with those of our allies, particularly the United States and the United Kingdom. With this, the government has always concurred and much is being done along these lines. As a matter of fact, when the Right Hon. Duncan Sandys, minister of supply in the United Kingdom government, was in Canada a few weeks ago, this subject was given a great deal of attention. Because of the nature of our aircraft industry, we are in a good position to pool our industrial knowledge with our allies. Nearly every one of our important


aircraft or component companies is affiliated with an outstanding American or British firm and therefore is in a position to draw on the information available to the parent company. This is true of Canadair, a subsidiary of General Dynamics; A. V. Roe and Canadian Steel Improvement, members of the Hawker-Siddeley group; Fairey Aviation, de Havilland, Sperry Gyroscope, Lucas-Rotax, and so on.
Our aircraft program is a good example of how we utilize all available know-how and developments. After the R.C.A.F. establishes an operational requirement, a survey is made of planes either in production or at the development stage, both in the United States and in the United Kingdom, as well as in Canada. If, as a result of this survey, undertaken jointly by D.D.P. and D.N.D., the R.C.A.F. is able to find a plane that suits their needs, we are asked to take the necessary procurement action. Normally, we have two alternatives-either to purchase from another country or produce in Canada.
Naturally, we prefer to manufacture in Canada, for reasons that I need not go into at this time. However, if Canadian production would not be economical because of the limited requirements, we do not hesitate to import. This latter policy has been followed in the case of the Banshees, the Neptunes, and the helicopters which we have ordered from the United States.
Where Canadian production appears feasible, such production may be based either on a licensing agreement, from another manufacturer or design and development by a Canadian company. In the first instance, the department secures a licence agreement, and a Canadian manufacturer is given a production order. This was done for the F-86 Sabre, for the T-33, and now for the Bristol Britannia. It is true that by following this practice we eliminate development costs. On the other 'band, we are faced with licence fees that are in reality a payment in support of the development staff of an aircraft industry in another country. There is no question that aircraft design and development is expensive. However, if we are to attain any degree of industrial maturity, we must encourage a certain amount of this type of development in Canada. This we have done, with a good measure of success in the case of the Canuck fighter and the Orenda engine, but we are limiting our activities to those areas in which we have a special interest and where Canadian requirements indicate the desirability of an independent approach.
On the subject of Canadian aircraft production, there is one statement which I believe will be of interest to the committee and that is that every firm with which we are

doing business is producing according to schedule. These schedules are drawn up by the department with a number of factors in mind. First, of course, come the requirements of the armed services; second, the availability of components, particularly imported components; third, the question of plant loadings in order to avoid peak employment followed by heavy laying-off of help, and finally and of the utmost importance, the level of economic production.
During the first two years of the aircraft program, our major concern was to get production started. This entailed the selection and, in several instances, the creation of facilities. It meant securing complicated machine tools and a number of key materials which were in short supply throughout the free world. Finally, good management teams and skilled labour forces had to be developed. Having completed the build-up of a sizeable aircraft industry in Canada, it has been possible during the last year to place even more emphasis on economy of production. Recent studies show that on any basis of comparison, our major airframe and aeroengine producers compare favourably with the best on this continent from the point of view of efficiency and economy. This is not only a credit to the producers of the aircraft and engines-it applies equally well to our component manufacturers. Today, we have virtually no airframe, aero-engine or component production in Canada on a cost-plus basis. In most cases, we have incentive type contracts, and, as a result, costs to the government are steadily decreasing.
Other characteristics of our aircraft industry today are its diversification and its dispersal across Canada. Apart from airframes, we are producing both jet and reciprocating engines. Components in production include engine blades, precision bearings, aircraft fittings, fuel systems, and a fair range of aircraft instruments. Considerable work is also being done on materials required to meet the exacting requirements of high speeds and temperatures. Titanium in particular is receiving a good deal of attention.
As far as dispersal is concerned, we have tried to ensure that our aircraft facilities are located in such a way as to service aircraft no matter where they are located in Canada. As a result we have important plants in Halifax and Amherst, Nova Scotia; St. Jean, Quebec; Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, Fort Erie, Fort William, Winnipeg, Calgary, Edmonton and Vancouver.
Now I would like to turn to our shipbuilding program. Without going into detail, this program may be divided into four parts, that is, frigate conversion, the Arctic patrol
Supply-Defence Production vessel, the minesweepers, and the destroyer escort vessels. What may not be realized is that these four parts of the program actually represent four major and complex development projects. The basis on which we decided to embark on this development and production program is the same as the one we used for the aircraft program when we found no one else producing a plane to meet our requirements. After looking around, we found that no one else was working on the type of ship that we needed to perform our anti-submarine role, and so we had to do our own development. Furthermore, we decided that production in Canada, including the major components, was desirable in order to maintain a nucleus of a naval shipbuilding industry which would be available in time of emergency.
Considerable progress has been made. The original conversion program will be completed this year, and from a design and construction point of view this has been practically equivalent to producing new ships. The Arctic patrol vessel will be commissioned next month. Of the original fourteen minesweepers, all have been launched, ten have been delivered, and the remainder will be completed by this fall. As some of these ships are being made available to our NATO partners under the mutual aid program, replacement orders have been placed with the shipyards. These will be of an improved design and able to cope with the latest developments in magnetic and acoustic mines.
We now have some cost experience in the production of this type of ship, and we are therefore anxious to place incentive type rather than cost-plus contracts for these additional minesweepers, thus ensuring the greatest possible economy of production.
On the other hand, it must be recognized that it is more difficult to establish a satisfactory target price for a ship, when only one or two are built in any one shipyard, than for a production line item, such as aircraft or ammunition, where it is reasonably easy to establish basic costs, learning curves, and so forth.
Some hon. members have commented on the apparent delays in the escort vessel program. This has been a very challenging undertaking. This ship is new, it is amazingly complex, and it embodies the latest developments of both the United States and the United Kingdom. It is designed to fulfil an anti-submarine role and during the last few years there has been a great deal of development in the field of submarines and torpedoes. Hence, the design of our anti-submarine vessel has been subject to constant change in order to keep pace.

Supply-Defence Production
When one considers the small number of qualified people we had in Canada in 1950 to cope with essentially four separate naval design projects, it is interesting to compare our performance with other countries that have had a great deal of experience in this field. Both the United States and the United Kingdom have recently commissioned new ships which, from a design and construction point of view, may be considered comparable to our escort vessels. The United States experience was that six years elapsed from the commencement of design to the delivery of the prototype. A similar program in the United Kingdom took six and one-half years. The design work on our escort vessel began in 1949 and the first delivery is expected next year-in other words, just under seven years. I believe that any discrepancies between actual and forecast performance are due not so much to abnormal production difficulties as to unrealistic forecasts.
Turning to guns and ammunition, there is one point that I would like to make clear. It will be recalled that approximately three years ago a decision was taken to standardize to a large extent on United States army equipment rather than the United Kingdom type which we had previously used. From a production point of view, this created a number of special problems in the guns and ammunition field.
In the United States, the requirements of Korea sparked an intensive drive to update and improve their basic weapons and ammunition. Consequently, instead of adopting equipment that was of a fixed design and in current production, we found ourselves trying to reproduce guns and ammunition that were undergoing rapid and radical development. As a result, there were inordinate delays in securing complete manufacturing drawings. This situation has now improved greatly. However, it has also been necessary to acquire detailed manufacturing data. This is being accomplished by our Canadian producers visiting production sites in the United States, and in this connection we have had the very best co-operation.
I do not want to leave the impression that we are not actually producing in these fields. Several natures of ammunition are being supplied from Canadian production to our own services, to the United States, and to our NATO allies as part of our mutual aid program. Production at the small arms plant of Canadian Arsenals at Long Branch is going very well. Sorel Industries have completed a large order of 120 millimeter guns for the United States army and are producing three-inch 50 calibre guns both for


the Canadian and United States navies in advance of agreed schedules. However, in some instances, progress has been slow, but I hope that I have given the committee some idea of the special problems that we have encountered.
The final important segment of our production program is in the field of electronics. Canadian industry has continued to expand its facilities for the manufacture of electronic defence equipment during the past year. This expansion has paralleled an unprecedented increase of commercial facilities for the manufacture of home television sets, with an estimated output of 450,000 units for the current year, as compared with approximately one-tenth of this output three years ago. These additional facilities for both defence and commercial work have broadened the available sources of supply for the department, and it has been possible to obtain competitive tenders on much of the equipment required by the services, with resultant economies.
Naturally, a great deal of our activity in this field is in connection with our aircraft, ship, and gun programs. However, with the additional emphasis being placed on continental defence and interception in the north, there are heavier requirements for Canadian radar and communications equipment. In all discussions with the United States authorities regarding joint plans for northern defence we have insisted that the Canadian electronics, communications, and construction industries be given full opportunity to participate in the program, irrespective of the basis of cost sharing between the two countries.
Apart from the production aspects of the program, there are two other main facets: construction and general purchasing. Defence Construction Limited, as hon. members will recall, has been responsible for defence construction, but in the past it has to a large extent utilized the services of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to supervise the actual projects. Although this arrangement proved eminently satisfactory, the recent amendments to the National Housing Act placed an additional work load on Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and, consequently, it was deemed advisable for Defence Construction Limited to take full responsibility for defence construction with the exception of the married quarters and school program, which will remain with C.M.H.C. The Department of National Defence estimates indicate that a large portion of our defence construction now either is completed or will be completed this year. However, there are a number of projects just getting under way, Gagetown being the most important.

Hon. members who have properly stressed the importance of getting the best return for our defence dollar will be glad to know that in the last few months we have noted increasing competition for defence construction contracts, a condition that will inevitably bring about lower costs.
We have made excellent progress in the field of mechanical transport. By the end of the last fiscal year, that branch had placed orders covering most of the armed services' requirements for military and special purpose vehicles and, as a result, its major function became the procurement of commercial type vehicles. Inasmuch as this is the type of procurement normally carried out by our general purchasing branch, it was decided, in the interests of economy, to merge the two branches into an augmented general purchasing branch.
In the first two years of the program the major work of this branch was in connection with the initial outfitting of the troops and the building up of clothing and equipment stockpiles. This has now been largely completed and current purchases are mainly to satisfy maintenance requirements. On the other hand, as additional vehicles, ships, and aircraft are brought into service, requirements for fuel and maintenance equipment have increased. Another important phase of the work of the general purchasing branch is the procurement carried out through its district offices. As service establishments are developed across Canada, the local purchasing activities of the 14 district offices located across Canada from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Victoria, British Columbia, have increased. In the first three months of 1954, these district offices have issued nearly 35,000 purchase documents, covering contracts totalling in excess of $14,500,000.
By far the greatest change in the defence production scene during the last two years has been in the field of strategic materials. It will be recalled that when the accelerated defence program was launched three years ago, strategic materials were generally in short supply and, through the agency of the international materials conference, international allocations were established for a number of commodities. This, of course, necessitated controls over production and distribution in Canada and in order to administer these programs we had at one time a materials branch, consisting of six divisions covering steel, non-ferrous metals, chemicals, petroleum, newsprint and priorities. Gradually, as circumstances permitted, we relaxed controls and decreased the personnel of the
Supply-Defence Production branch until, by the end of the last calendar year, we were able to abolish all controls and the materials branch itself.
This brings us to the organization of the Department of Defence Production. After its establishment on April 1, 1951, it reached a peak strength of 1,762 on June 30, 1952. On May 31 of this year, the number was 1,539. This reduction was largely due to the abolition of the materials branch to which I have already made reference. For the information of the committee, charts indicating the organization of the department as of June 1 have been distributed to all hon. members.
When the Minister of National Defence was discussing his estimates, he spoke of the long-range planning of the NATO alliance, which has been described as the "long haul" approach. He also indicated that, although modest reductions in defence budgets were possible during the next few years, current commitments and the need to maintain our position of active and effective preparedness would require substantial defence expenditures for a number of years.
This obviously means that there will be a continuing requirement for an efficient procurement organization. In the early stages of the department's history, we secured the loan of a number of experienced men from industry, who either directed our various production and material branches or provided valuable assistance in other capacities. At one time, we had as many as 99 so-called "dollar a year" men in the department. Today, only two of our branches are being directed by other than career civil servants, and the total number of industry men on loan has been reduced to 10. These men from industry, who have given generously of their time and experience, have made a very real contribution to the defence effort. But it is obvious that, in the long run, we must depend on career civil servants to staff a government department.
We have been making every effort to develop a sound organization on this basis. However, we find that, because the life of the department is limited to five years under the terms of the Defence Production Act, there is a tendency for some members of the staff to seek other employment that apparently provides more security. Furthermore, we have found that the temporary nature of the department is often a deterrent to well qualified men who have considered joining us.
Under these circumstances, I believe that it is appropriate to announce now that it is

Supply-Defence Production the government's intention to seek, during the next session of parliament, an amendment to the Defence Production Act which will put the life of the department on a more permanent basis.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the committee has listened with interest to the review which the minister has just read concerning the operations of the Department of Defence Production and some rather significant changes that have appeared in the program of that department and the conditions with which it has to deal in Canadian industry. I am sure that the committee was glad also to hear what the minister read to us concerning deliveries and also concerning the emergence now of increased competition. I think no one will be surprised at that situation having regard to the fact that competition now is so much keener throughout Canadian industry in general. So far as the government purchasing program is concerned, it is a factor that will undoubtedly react to the advantage of the taxpayer. As I proceed I hope to make a comment concerning the announcement in the final paragraph of the minister's statement, which, it seems to me, is of no little importance.
The estimates of this department this year call for an expenditure of $40 million as against appropriations for the year ended March 31, 1954, of $73 million. On the surface this represents in the appropriations of the department a reduction of $33 million which parallels a simplification of the task of the department and an advance in the government's purchasing program on account of defence.
The task of the department is indeed an important one. This department came into existence on April 1, 1951. It has therefore now been in existence for approximately three years and three months and the expenditures on account of defence which have been made through this department in that period are now approaching the $5 billion mark.
The minister has made a comment upon the reduction in the staff of the department this year. There has, of course, been a notable reduction in the tasks, functions and difficulties of the department as a result of the developments within the past year or fifteen months. The minister has made reference to the marked improvement in the supply of strategic materials, which improvement made it possible on December 31, 1953, to discontinue the remaining controls and indeed the materials division of the department.
The temporary nature of the department, to which the minister made reference, has


unquestionably been a factor in the minds of some of the senior men in the department. No one needs to have many contacts with men holding responsible senior positions in the department in order to realize that what the minister has called the temporary nature of the department has had an unsettling effect on the minds of many of those senior officials with regard to their continuation in the service of the department. I am not going to attempt to pass judgment upon the amendment which the minister indicates the government will introduce at the next session of parliament. However, 1 say this. It is a most interesting announcement and the problem with which, I take it, the amendment is intended to deal is a significant one to which attention must be directed.
Our thoughts in relation to our task as a committee of supply this morning are, I think, related not simply to the matters of supply of materials to which the minister has made reference or to improving deliveries. In addition we are concerned about the policy followed within the department. The minister has not made any extended comment on the policy within the department. I propose to speak briefly concerning various phases of that policy as we have known it in the past and to ask the minister, at the appropriate time, for an adequate statement as to policy and as to whether in this and other respects there has been any change or development in the policy of the department.
My first question is in relation to policy as it affects the Department of National Defence. Recently we have spent several days reviewing the estimates of the Department of National Defence. Yesterday we spent an extremely long day, completing that review only at a late hour last night. It is not my intention to go over any of that ground, but as to the relationship between these two departments there is much that the committee yet needs to be told.
Is the relationship between the two departments what it was when the estimates of this department were before the House of Commons for review a year ago? That is my first question in this regard. We were told by the minister himself a year ago on a similar occasion that in effect the Department of Defence Production has nothing to do with and takes no responsibility in relation to quantities or, indeed, the nature of purchases, and that it simply accepts requisitions from the Department of National Defence and then proceeds to fill those requirements by purchase or by contract. The relationship between the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production

was significantly stated by the minister on May 7, 1953, at page 4923 of Hansard, in these words:
It would upset the relations between the two departments if we questioned the requirements of the services, and it is not our business to do so. If the services say they need a gold-plated piano, it is our duty to buy it.
I ask the minister if the relationship between the two departments is today as it was on May 7, 1953. Is it still the function of the Department of Defence Production simply to receive requests from the Department of National Defence and to fill them willy-nilly without question? Indeed, Mr. Chairman, with all apologies to Tennyson and "The Charge of the Light Brigade", one can say that the function of the Department of Defence Production, as indicated by the minister in this passage last year, might be put in this way:
Theirs not to reason why.
Theirs but to build and buy.
When expenditures of some $5 billion are made in a period of three years and three months I think the house is entitled to expect scrutiny of these purchases, not simply the terms on which the minister's department is purchasing them but as to the necessity for these vast purchases that have been made. In no other way is there going to be any pretence of protecting the interests of the taxpayers.
The next question I wish to ask in relation to the policy of the department as to where they are making their purchases and as to what direction, if any, they are seeking to give to their purchasing policy. Last year the minister declared the policy of the department in this respect to be, first, to purchase in Canada where possible, that is to say, where goods are available on the same or, I take it, approximately the same terms as they can be purchased from abroad; second, to direct purchases to the United Kingdom, and in the third place to the United States. I ask if that is still the policy of the department. I do not think there will be any quarrel with that as a statement of policy, but we will wish to know a good deal more than we have been told either in the statement read by the minister this morning or in the annual report of the department for the calendar year 1953 as to what has been done in fulfilment of such a policy.
The report of the department for the calendar year 1953 contains at pages 45 to 51 some statistical information concerning purchases by the department either by way of defence orders or defence procurement expenses as well as approved projects for capital assistance. As to purchases in the United Kingdom, I think I do not need to labour the point
Supply-Defence Production that here is one place where we can at the same time purchase wisely and assist our export policy. Purchases from the United Kingdom have this double advantage under present conditions.
I referred a few days ago to the statement made on April 14 by Mr. James S. Duncan, chairman of the dollar-sterling trade council, in which he drew attention to the advantages that would flow to Canada in seeking to increase her export trade if we could transfer even a modest percentage of our present huge purchases in the United States to the United Kingdom. These were his words:
Based on last year's trade pattern, if we could transfer only 7 per cent of our imports from the United States to the United Kingdom, it would eliminate Britain's trade deficit with us and put her in a much better position to buy our products.
Mr. Duncan went on to state that the purpose of the dollar-sterling trade council is to assist in this 7 per cent transfer of Canadian imports from the United States to the United Kingdom. It was graphically put by Mr. Peter Thorneycroft, president of the British board of trade, in his recent visit to Canada when, indicating Britain's wish to increase her purchases from Canada and also her capital investments in Canada, he said in a picturesque phrase, "You cannot invest a deficit". It is hardly to be expected that Britain, looking at our trade relationships in the past, is going to arrive at the point where she sells to Canada more than she buys from Canada. Historically Canada has had a substantial export surplus in her trade relationships with the United Kingdom just as in her trade relationships with the United States historically she has had an import surplus. But much could be done to the advantage of Canada to reduce the extent of Canada's export surplus with Great Britain by transferring much of our purchases abroad from the United States to the United Kingdom. Here in the matter of defence procurement we have an opportunity to help to rectify that balance. To the extent to which purchases are not possible in Canada, then certainly every opportunity should be given to make those purchases in the United Kingdom rather than elsewhere. Looking at the figures contained in the report of the Department of Defence Production for the calendar year 1953, we can only conclude that the purchases made by this department and the orders placed in the United Kingdom are disappointingly small.
Looking at the tables beginning at page 46 of the report in relationship to total Canadian defence orders, we see that in the year 1952 Canada's total defence orders amounted to $1,409 million. I will give simply round

Supply-Defence Production figures. Of that total 90 per cent were placed in Canada, a total of $1,262 million. Orders placed in the United States come next, $78 million, or 5| per cent. Orders placed in the United Kingdom were just $63 million, or only 4i- per cent of the total. If we look at the 1953 figures we will see that the total of defence orders was substantially reduced last year. The total dropped from $1,409 million in 1952 to $811 million in 1953. That of course is to be explained by the fact that these are defence orders placed and the bulk of the placement program of course was accelerated in the year 1952.
Of these orders in 1953 we see that $716 million worth were placed in Canada, or 88| per cent, in the United States $61 million or 71 per cent of the total, and in the United Kingdom just $33 million, or only 4 per cent of the total. The total of defence orders placed in the United Kingdom compared with the United States was indeed small enough in 1952, $63 million; in 1953, out of a smaller total, that figure had dropped to $33 million or just one half of the total of orders placed in the previous year.
If we look at the expenditures on defence procurement, for which figures are also contained in the tables on the pages I have mentioned in this report, we will see that in 1952 the expenditure totalled $1,095 million, of which, according to my arithmetic, 86 per cent were placed in Canada, 12 per cent or $132 million were expended in the United States, and only 2 per cent or $22 million were placed in the United Kingdom. In the year 1953 the total of expenditures on defence procurement had increased to $1,174 million, of which 85 per cent was placed in Canada; $130 million or 11 per cent were placed in the United States and $49 million or 4 per cent were placed in the United Kingdom. It is to be seen that while the actual expenditures on defence procurement in the United Kingdom were doubled in 1953 over 1952, nevertheless the total figure in 1953 of $49 million of expenditure on defence procurement in the United Kingdom is still a very small fraction of the total, being only 4 per cent.

friend tell me where he is getting his figures, Mr. Chairman. My figures show that in 1953 $33 million was expended in the United Kingdom and $61 million in the United States.

The minister is away behind me. I had already dealt with Canadian defence orders. He is reading the figures on pages 46 and 47 of the departmental report.
I went on from there to deal with the figures for defence procurement which are to be


found on pages 49 and 50 of the report. He will see the figures I have been dealing with latterly are the figures for defence procurement.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Oh, I see.

There has not been any
unwillingness on the part of the United Kingdom to extend its sales of defence materials or equipment to Canada. On the contrary there has been evidence of the appreciation in the United Kingdom of the opportunity that exists and the desirability, in the interests of the United Kingdom as well as of Canada, of taking every advantage of the opportunity that exists through this vast spending program.
I have in my hand a Canadian Press dispatch, dated May 20, 1953, from Ottawa, and it reads in part as follows:
The British government today announced it is taking new action to step up Canada's defence orders with Britain, the United Kingdom information office here said. First of a number of measures will be the assignment of two officials to Canada to deal with requirements of the Canadian armed forces that could be supplied by Britain.
And so the dispatch proceeds. One can find other dispatches emanating from United Kingdom sources of high authority, indicating the wish of the United Kingdom government and of United Kingdom manufacturers to meet the needs existing in Canada wherever there is an opportunity given to them of doing so. Here is a golden opportunity where we are making the purchases anyway, and it does not mean any further drain upon the resources of the Canadian taxpayer, either by way of loans, gifts or preferences, in aiding Britain. In the case of goods or equipment that cannot be found in Canada, let us direct those purchases to the United Kingdom, and in that way furnish the United Kingdom with the needed dollars with which she may increase her purchases from Canada of wheat and other goods which we have here in such surplus supply.
To the extent to which this large spending program has progressed wherever purchases have been made in the United States that could have been made in the United Kingdom, we had lost what I think, and perhaps all members will agree, is a valuable opportunity to help Britain increase her purchases from Canada. The minister made an interesting speech in Montreal last week indicating a degree of concern which we have not always found present in the minister's speeches, about the desirability of closer trading relations with the United Kingdom. Here is an opportunity, without putting any additional burden upon the Canadian taxpayer, in cases where purchases cannot be

made within our own borders, to help ourselves by making these purchases from United Kingdom sources rather than from the United States and elsewhere.
I point out at the same time, Mr. Chairman, that it is evident from the report of the department that our expenditures in the United States are very great, whether by way of defence orders placed or procurement expenditures and orders. The total orders and expenditures in the United States in 1953 have held up more than the orders and expenditures made either in Canada or in the United Kingdom.
I am next led to ask about the position and policy with respect to the purchase of machine tools. We had some discussion a year ago in connection with the estimates of this department as to the progress in connection with the acquisition of machine tools and the policy in reference to the place of the purchase of those important factors in our defence program. If one looks at page 21 of the report, one will see that in 1953 "the United States remained the largest single source of supply for machine tools". Page DD-16 of the public accounts for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1953, seems to bear this out. It would be interesting to know in this connection to what extent the department has been acquiring small machine tools from German sources and whether those purchases could have been made from United Kingdom sources.
I next turn to the subject of capital assistance. Capital assistance has played an important role in the defence program. The minister had, I believe, nothing to say in his statement this morning concerning capital assistance. We had questions to ask and something to say on this subject last year. The estimates of the department indicate that the program of capital assistance faces quite a substantial curtailment this year. The amount asked in this connection this year is $25 million as compared with $60 million for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954. Last year we sought to ascertain how the program of capital assistance, under the government's administration, was dovetailing with what appeared to us in the official opposition to be a necessary policy with respect to our defence program in this regard.
I have indicated how, in our view, purchases which we must make abroad could, with great advantage to Canada, be made in the United Kingdom.
I should like now to say that, as to purchases within Canada, there is great advantage to be derived from the widest possible dissemination of those purchases
Supply-Defence Production throughout Canada with a view to distributing the advantages that come from a program of this kind. No one is suggesting any serious departure from the rules of economics or of sound buying; but, Mr. Chairman, the minister has never yet convinced us that within the scope of purchases being made within Canada he is taking advantage of the opportunity that is placed in his hands of bringing advantage to provinces other than the central provinces in the distribution of these defence orders.
Here was an opportunity, perhaps the opportunity of a lifetime-an opportunity at any rate which has not existed at any time in Canada's history, with the exception of the period of world war II-to assist in strengthening the economies of the other provinces by placing defence orders there. Think what it would mean to the economy of the maritime provinces, the economy of Manitoba and the economy of other provinces, by way of strengthening secondary industry in those provinces and providing a broader foundation for economic life in those provinces, if to a great extent this program of defence purchasing were distributed with advantage to those provinces, rather than having it concentrated in central Canada.
The information on the subject is deplorably scant. Last year one turned to the public accounts, for lack of any other authentic source of information. I pointed out last year that, if one is to judge by the head offices of the corporations with which these defence orders were placed, the program was largely confined to the central provinces. The minister took issue with that basis of determining where the orders were being filled. He said, "You cannot tell, entirely, from the location of the head offices of companies, where orders are being filled or where subcontracts let by those contractors are being placed". That may be so. But if the minister has a better or a more reliable way of determining where the advantages of this defence purchasing program are being distributed, then I wish he would tell the house about it.
This morning he said something very brief and very vague about the distribution of purchases. Let us have more information on the subject. We have had enough discussion and enough consideration of the subject in times past to want some detailed information about it. Indeed when from time to time we have asked for information of this kind we have been put off with vague generalities to the effect that the department does not keep records in that way.
On what sound statistical information has the minister made this vague statement this morning about the distribution of the benefits of the purchasing program within Canada?

Supply-Defence Production Until he does give some proper information in this respect, I can only refer to the public accounts in relation to his department, and note from that source that for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1953, we find at pages DD-3, 4 and 5, looking at the provision for "capital assistance for the construction, acquisition, extension or improvement of capital equipment or works by private contractors engaged in defence contracts, or by crown plants operated on a management-fee basis, or by crown companies under direction of the Minister of Defence Production, subject to approval of treasury board", that, out of a total of allotments of $110 million, and expenditures of roughly $78 million, the number of companies or contractors receiving capital assistance was 84. The information discloses that the head offices of 73 of these 84 companies were located in the two central provinces, with only three in Nova Scotia, one in New Brunswick, three in Alberta, two in British Columbia and two in Manitoba.
That does not contain very eloquent testimony either to the success or, indeed, to the effort of the government in seeking to distribute those purchases more widely throughout Canada. I live in one of the central provinces. I know there are advantages in the matter of the fulfilment of orders from the fact that there is a concentration in those central provinces of industrial capacity. But, Mr. Chairman, speaking not as a central Canadian, but as a Canadian, I say that here is a great and extraordinary opportunity given to the government to strengthen the economy, particularly the secondary industry, in the other provinces, and I am thinking particularly of provinces such as the maritimes, Manitoba and others. I am afraid that, in the light of available information, it looks as though the government is allowing this opportunity to slip away without advantage to these other provinces whose economies could be strengthened in the course of a program of this kind, without putting the slightest additional burden upon any Canadian taxpayer.
In this program upon which we are embarked we wish to see, so far as possible, that purchases are made within Canada, when the supply is available here. If that is our position, then why can we not, to a far greater extent than is indicated by these figures, direct those purchases so that they will be of general advantage to all of Canada?
In conclusion I come to several matters of a more specific nature. Those of us in this part of the house have always been concerned about the provisions of section 17 of the Defence Production Act, as it is set out in chapter 4 of the statutes of 1951, second


session. This is the statute that established this department, and from which it derives its wide powers. Under section 17 (1) (e) of this statute, we see that-
(e) a contract may be entered into by the minister without the approval of the governor in council if
(i)	in the opinion of the minister, the contract must be entered into immediately in the interests of defence,
(ii)	the estimated expenditure, loan or guarantee does not exceed twenty-five thousand dollars, or
(iii)	competitive tenders have been obtained and the lowest tender, involving an estimated expenditure not exceeding fifty thousand dollars, is accepted.
This section, of course, covers more than purchases without tender. But the provisions of the section have always been so broad that each year we have made it our business to look for an extended and detailed report on the subject. What is the extent to which the department is making purchases now without calling for tenders? Now that the early feverish haste in launching this program of defence procurement may be said to have passed, is it not possible to proceed by more orthodox and established methods in making purchases or awarding contracts?
In this regard one listened with interest to the statement of the minister this morning that the department is now departing from its previous practice of awarding contracts on a cost-plus basis. That was welcome news, particularly to those of us including yourself, Mr. Chairman, who during the 1953 session served on the special committee on defence expenditure. We were not the least bit happy about the wide extent to which contracts were being awarded through this department and its corporate creations on a cost-plus basis. To the extent to which the department is now awarding what the minister has this morning called "incentive contracts", in place of cost-plus contracts, we shall acclaim that as a step forward. We wish to know more about it; we wish to know how far this trend has gone. We do not make any attempt to disguise our dislike for the kind of contracts that have been awarded by the department in the past.
In the next place, Mr. Chairman, we want more information about the operations of the revolving fund within this department. Section 16 of the Defence Production Act makes provision for "a defence production revolving fund". In that fund there is a working capital of $150 million turning over in the department today. The annual report of the department on this point is very sketchy indeed. We ask for more information on that point.
We next ask for more information concerning the policy of the department in relation

to disposal or retention of crown assets. I am thinking in this respect in the first place, but not entirely, of crown-owned plants.
Within the past year a very large plant has been disposed of by the government. Last September an announcement was made that the government-owned Orenda jet engine plant at Malton had been sold to the A. V. Roe Canada Limited at a sale price of somewhere, according to newspaper reports, between $17 million and $17,500,000. According to the newspaper reports the original cost of the plant was $35 million, and the government-

speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman.
-retains ownership of about $17 million worth of equipment in the plant.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The cost the hon. member gave included the equipment. The equipment was not sold.

Yes. That is what I was saying. That is the burden of the report which I have just been reading. The plant was sold for a price, as mentioned here, of between $17 million and $17,500,000. The total cost of the plant and equipment was $35 million and the government is retaining ownership of about $17 million worth of equipment in the plant. That is a very substantial sale, Mr. Chairman, and it naturally leads one to ask questions as to the policy of the government in this respect. Is it policy to dispose of crown-owned plants? If so, what are the terms or objectives which guide the government in relation to sales? In this case the sale was made to the corporation which was managing the plant on a management-fee basis. One can see that if the government did decide to dispose of the plant, that corporation was the natural purchaser if terms were reasonable and every effort had been made to assure that the taxpayers' interests were adequately protected in the sale.
I ask the government as to policy in this respect. Are other purchases in contemplation? What steps are being taken to assure that in the case of disposals of plants the full value of those plants is being realized in the sale price?
I ask generally about policy in regard to sale of crown assets. I have referred particularly to crown-owned plants. In conclusion I turn to crown-owned assets of another nature. We have a corporation which functions under this department known as the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. Its function, as it has been described in times past, is to dispose of crown assets that are surplus to the crown requirements. We have
Supply-Defence Production been assured in the past that before any steps are taken through that corporation to dispose of crown assets every proper inquiry is made to determine whether those assets are required not simply in this department but in other departments of government.
Here is a department that is expending billions of dollars of the Canadian taxpayers' money, because this money has all come out of the taxpayer; none of it has been borrowed; none of it is to be paid for by future generations; all of it is being paid for by the taxpayers of 1951, 1952, 1953 and now 1954.
What is the policy in this respect? How is the policy being administered by the department? Well, I hope the case to which I am about to refer, Mr. Chairman, is not an example of the way in which the government is discharging its responsibilities in this respect. I hold in my hand an invitation to tender, issued by the Department of Defence Production, and dated March 30, 1954, inviting the submission of tenders for certain "automotive spares (bearings) ", the tenders to be addressed to the secretary of the department at Ottawa and to be received by him not later than four o'clock p.m. on April 27, 1954. Attached to this invitation to tender are three sheets setting forth a considerable number of bearings, all identified by certain well-recognized trade designations. In most cases the bearings specified are either SKF or Timken bearings. In some cases they are either Timkens, Hyatts, New Progress, or Bantam and some other bearings, but many of them are Timken bearings, each of which bears a number designation which refers to and identifies a standard form of bearing produced by the Timken Roller Bearing Company. They are completely standardized, as all hon. members will appreciate. Every one of them has a trade number identifying it. The quantities required vary greatly. I have not counted them but I presume there are about sixty different types of roller bearings that were to be purchased in accordance with this tender. The quantities purchased of each kind of bearing rise from 3 of a minimum to, I think, a maximum of 28,365. Therefore in the total number of bearings on which those in the trade are being invited to tender we have some scores and scores of thousands of bearings. In other words, this is not a small matter.
I also hold in my hand, Mr. Chairman, an advertisement put out by a Toronto firm which is engaged in the sale of used automobile parts as well as new ones. This firm put out a letter to the trade dated March 30, 1954, advertising for sale "bearings Timken, SKF, Hyatt" and many others.

No one, Mr. Chairman, expects the minister to be a superman or the department he heads to have superman wisdom or efficiency. But I think we are entitled, as a House of Commons being invited to vote billions of dollars of the Canadian taxpayers' money, and hard-earned money in practically every case, to expect a higher degree of efficiency than is displayed here, particularly when the government is disposing of surplus and then turning around and purchasing the very same thing by public tender and, as we well know in such a case, at a substantially higher cost.
I repeat what I said in introducing my review of the information in reference to this case, namely, that one hopes this is not an example of the way in which the operations of the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation and the purchasing activities of the Department of Defence Production are correlated, because there is no evidence here of any correlation whatever. So, Mr. Chairman, we will expect something much stricter, much tighter, and much more efficient in the way of the administration of the department than that case indicates is the situation.

Yes. I am sending over to
the minister, Mr. Chairman, the entire papers to which I have referred. There are some seven or eight pages.
Let me say in conclusion, Mr. Chairman, that the powers wielded by the Department of Defence Production are very great. When you place it within the power of a government department in peacetime to make purchases in a matter of three years aggregating a figure approaching $5 billion, I do not need to tell any hon. member of this house that you are placing in the hands of the government, and particularly in the hands of the minister who heads that department, vast powers over the economy of this country.
It is an unhappy circumstance that the world being the kind of uneasy, turbulent, and unsafe place in which we find ourselves, Mr. Chairman, it is necessary to undertake a defence program as vast and costly as this one is. But the very least that the House of Commons ought to do in these matters is to

insist upon the observance of sound and fair policies in these matters, and that the vast economic power which is placed in the hands of the government under this program shall not be arbitrarily wielded to the disadvantage of individuals in Canada. Where there are advantages they should be widely distributed, and where orders are to be placed they should be placed on a fair and equal basis. The last thing in the world that could be justified is any form of discrimination or the wielding over the heads of manufacturers, and through them their workmen, of powers of this kind in an unfair manner.
And so, Mr. Chairman, while we have indicated the importance we attach to the functions of this department, we do call for a strict scrutiny. It is perhaps unfortunate that this year there has not been a committee charged with the responsibility of reviewing the transactions of this department. The fact is that we have had many committees this year, they have been discharging a heavy responsibility, and there is a limit to the number of committees that can operate efficiently in a single session. But apart from that, Mr. Chairman, I shall not need to remind you, as a member of the defence expenditure committee in 1953, that we had some very disappointing and frustrating experiences on that committee. The committee was not permitted to extend its review back beyond April 1, 1950, and the committee was never permitted to review the estimates of the department for the current year. It was permitted to review nothing but expenditures made in the past.
As a means of testing the propriety and fitness of the estimates of expenditures for the current year it had no competence whatever, for it lacked all power. The kind of committee that is needed, Mr. Chairman, to review the type of expenditure that is being made through this department on behalf of the Department of National Defence, expenditures that amount to very close to half of the national budget, is the type of committee which has an opportunity to review the estimates of expenditure for the current year and the proposed expenditure, not simply the expenditure made in the past. In that way and in that way alone will parliament really be in a position to discharge its duty to review the operations of this department effectively.

Mr. Chairman, I was interested to hear the minister tell us that the policy of granting cost-plus contracts has now yielded place to the granting of another type of contract which I believe he referred to as an incentive contract. Not
Supply-Defence Production only would I be interested but I would be relieved by that statement were it not that I remember hearing of other types of contracts that have been let by this and other governments which, in my simple-minded manner, I had imagined were in effect cost-plus contracts but as to which I was told I was quite mistaken and that they were, on the other hand, what were known at that time as target contracts.
They were an extremely interesting instrument of agreement, Mr. Chairman. Apparently a target contract was something like this. There was a certain figure at which it was presumed a contractor was supposed to aim; and when, as inevitably happened, he aimed at this price and hit not the bull's-eye but a point away out on the outer part of the target, then the procedure was to move the bull's-eye out to where he had hit. For instance, I recall asking earlier in the session-a question about certain naval vessels that we had been constructing. I was interested in them because last year I was working in the yard that was producing these vessels and we saw them. They were these quite small wooden minesweepers. We had discovered that the target price had been $925,000. Later we heard rumours that it had been increased to $1,600,000. Hence I put a question on the order paper when I became a member-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend wants to mislead the committee. There was never a target-price contract placed for a minesweeper until these last three months. My hon. friend is talking about estimates of costs. He is not talking about contract price, and I wish he would not call them that.

All right, Mr. Chairman; we will call them estimates of cost. The estimate of cost was so far out that, instead of costing $925,000, they were to cost $1,600,000, according to the answer I received in reply to the question I put on the order paper.

Then there is another question that is in my mind when I read the report of the Department of Defence Production and when I find on page 14 that up to the end of 1953 -I hope the minister will correct me if I am wrong; I am assuming that is the period from the establishment of the department to the end of 1953-certificates had been issued covering some $665 million worth of capital investment in facilities for the production of both basic materials and defence supplies, thereby allowing additional benefits by way of income tax write-offs amounting to some $277 million. This is a reference, Mr. Chairman, to what is commonly known as accelerated depreciation. Of course it may be that that has been necessary in order to ensure the production of defence materials. However, when I read that I was reminded of another instance in which the taxpayers of Canada were asked by this government to forgo some of their legitimate income in order to aid another struggling company to produce materials for Canada's war effort. I refer to the Aluminum Company of Canada.
On that occasion we afforded them these additional benefits-as they are referred to in the report of the Department of Defence Production-to the tune of $177,359,956.06. Mr. Chairman, it may perhaps have been


necessary to do that. Perhaps it was necessary because we were asking the Aluminum Company of Canada to expand their facilities to an extent that would be far greater than anything for which they could find use after the war. In fact, as I recall it, that was the idea that was presented to the people of Canada. That is why they were asked to forgo approximately $177,000,000 of income in order that this company might be enabled to meet our wartime needs.
Mr. Chairman, somebody again made an estimate that was very wide of the mark. Hardly had the war ended than this same struggling company brought their approximately $177 million plus several hundred million dollars more up into British Columbia to expand still further their facilities in a period that we have been given to believe would not provide any market for the expanded facilities at Arvida. Therefore, as I say, I have some doubts as to the possible necessity for this relinquishment of $277 million worth of income to the federal treasury.
Then in the next paragraph we are told of the $48 million that is being granted by way of capital assistance to private industry. Again, it may perhaps be necessary to grant this assistance to firms in order to get them to produce the materials that we require for our defence expenditures. But, Mr. Chairman, surely there is a reasonable case to be made out for this government's retaining, on behalf of the people of Canada, an equity in those industrial facilities for which we are providing the capital. Surely that is not an unreasonable proposition.

I certainly withdraw everything I have said. I am extremely glad to hear that. I was afraid that this was the same sort of assistance we had given

to the aluminum company. Now, Mr. Chairman, I am not, however, so particularly interested in these aspects of our defence production program. I do not think, for instance, there is anyone in this chamber, including the minister himself, who can tell us with any assurance that our $2 billion that is going to defence expenditures is being spent in the wisest manner possible. I think that is entirely a matter of opinion. I think the opinions may be based on very little information, and it may not be possible to get the information. Let us agree that they are doing the best they can in that regard; but let us, on the other hand, proceed to get some incidental benefits out of these wasteful and misguided expenditures, if there are any such in this department.
To that end I should like to direct the attention of the government to the policy that is now being pursued by the government of the United States. I have in my hand defence manpower policy No. 4 as revised on November 5, 1953. This defence manpower policy directive from the office of the President of the United States is designed to ensure that defence expenditures in the United States are placed with certain objectives in mind, one of them being the objective of maintaining, as they say here, "management and employee skills necessary to the fulfilment of government contracts and purchases", the idea being that there should be a consideration of the needs of industrial development and industrial employment in various parts of the United States in the placing of departmental orders. Paragraph 2 of this directive has this to say under the heading "purpose":
It is the purpose of this defence manpower policy No. 4 to direct attention to the potentialities of areas of substantial labour surplus, hereafter referred to as labour surplus areas, for the placement of procurement contracts or the location of new plants or facilities, and to assign responsibilities to specify departments and agencies of the government to carry out the policy stated below.
I may say that the definition of a labour surplus area for the purpose of this directive is an area in which the labour surplus is 6 per cent or over and an area in which there appears to be no immediate sign of improvement. With respect to the purposes the directive goes on to say that they are:
(b)	To maintain productive facilities;
(c)	To improve utilization of the nation's total manpower potential by making use of the manpower resources of each area;
(d)	To help assure timely delivery of required goods and services and to promote readiness for expanded effort by locating procurement where the needed manpower and facilities are fully available; and
(e)	To reduce the vulnerability of defence related and essential civilian industries to air attack in the event of war.
Supply-Defence Production
That last point is, I think, a very important consideration. It is only about a week or two ago that one of the military correspondents, I think it was Hanson Baldwin of the New York Times, pointed out this rather ominous fact, that one of the ways in which the Soviet union is gaining superiority over the United States and North America is that it is providing fewer effective aerial targets than we are on this continent, that they have been pursuing a deliberate and conscious policy of dispersal of industry all across the Eurasian continent. Here on this continent, unfortunately, we pursue a rather haphazard policy of allowing industrial development to take place wherever immediate existing economic circumstances cause it to arise, with the result that we have located in the lower Ontario area, as the hon. member for Eglinton pointed out, a concentration of industry which provides an ideal target for aerial attack.
I believe that here we have an opportunity not merely to disperse our industry or to develop industry across the country but an opportunity to do something that our American friends have not done hitherto and that they are now apparently trying to do, a rational reorganization of their industrial potential. I think we have an opportunity that we perhaps could have in no other way of really developing the productive capacities of this country in relation to population, resources and climate in a way in which no nation has hitherto had. I would urge very strongly on the minister and the government that they make this consideration one of their major considerations in the placement of defence production orders, and particularly in the decision as to areas in which there shall be investment in new productive facilities.
The history of the United States shows quite plainly that its modern industrial potential was developed in two major periods, that period comprised in the first world war and the period of the second world war, when enormous expansions and developments of American industry took place under the stimulus of defence production expenditures. It may be of course that informally our government is doing that type of thing, but the Department of Defence Production has received no direction from this parliament to follow out precisely the sort of program that is now being pursued in the United States of America.
Since the session began we have had a series of visits from representatives of the unemployed, who are now such a source of anxiety to us. We have had, moreover, appeals from members from different parts

Supply-Defence Production of the country with regard to the necessity for economic rehabilitation. I have no doubt that the hon. member for Cape Breton South will be dinning the necessities of his part of Canada into the minister's ears before this debate is over. I can think of no better way in which the government could combine the carrying out of its responsibilities for defence production with its more basic responsibility for the material welfare of the whole Dominion of Canada than by giving consideration to the deliberate development of industrial potential in those parts of Canada which are now either declining industrially or have not hitherto had any important industrial development.

Mr. Chairman, in taking part in this debate on the defence production estimates I wish to address my remarks to three matters particularly, the first of which is a question of policy. I should like to know how government policy in the matter of purchases differs today from what it was during the war years. I contend that industry has a right to know this. During the war, when we were very hard pressed for materials, goods and production, there was a definite policy of assistance. That certainly saw us through the war and was an excellent measure. The same minister is in charge of the department today. He did such a good job at that time that I was hoping that I could say that he had been able to continue to do so.
Today, however, it seems to be a matter of looking for the cheapest market. I am thinking particularly of an answer I received to a question I put in the house one day respecting the use of British Columbia plywood in the building of keels for six minesweepers that were built at Bellingham, Washington.
I finally received the answer. It indicated that an eastern firm had been given the contract, that it had been sublet to a Bellingham, Washington, firm, and that was all there was to it. I am not too happy about such a situation, especially in view of the fact that I understand a New Westminster firm submitted a tender which must have been refused. If it is going to be the policy of this government to buy wherever the market is cheapest, I believe that those men who are particularly interested in building up industry in our country should know about that.
The second factor also concerns policy, but is a matter of a more localized nature. There are very few west coast firms that receive contracts from the defence department. I am given to understand the reason is that our prices are too high. I wonder why that is the case? Is it the cost of labour 
or are there some particular factors that are involved? I should like to remind the minister that British Columbia dollars are poured into this particular government in some volume. While our bids might be high, on occasion they must be close enough to warrant spending more dollars in British Columbia for defence production than have been spent in the past.
There is one important factor in which I am rather interested in this respect, and that is to what degree have studies been made with a view to manufacturing an article on the western coast instead of manufacturing it in the eastern part of Canada and sending it to the west coast. We know that a good portion of this material must be sent to the west from time to time, and therefore it might just as well be produced at that point. What thought has been given to sending raw materials to the west or to the far eastern coast for that matter, and manufacturing the finished product that might be needed at that point rather than building it in various parts of the country and sending it to either the eastern or western coast. In the explosive world in which we live it could prove most unfortunate, and would be most unrealistic, to put all our eggs in one basket.
The third point I wish to mention is a major one in the minds of members from British Columbia and Alberta. It concerns the construction of a pipe line from the Peace river area in Alberta and British Columbia into the Vancouver district. I noted with some concern, as did most of the British Columbia members, I am sure, the decision of the federal power commission that they would not accept Westcoast Transmission Company's offer to build a line into the Pacific northwest. I was happy to note, though, that there is a 30-day waiting period for reconsideration of this decision. I would urge the minister to give consideration to our request and try to do something as quickly as possible, before this 30-day period is up, to enable this line to be built.
I do not believe that it is proper that the provinces of British Columbia and Alberta should be made to suffer because the West-coast Transmission people probably did not make as good a case as might have been made in trying to persuade the United States authorities to permit them to supply gas. On June 19, I believe, the hon. member for Macleod sent the minister a question in respect of this problem, and later the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra raised the question on the floor of the house. I am sure none of us are too happy about the responses we have received. I should like the minister to ask the United States authorities to review

the whole situation with a view to either changing their decision and accepting this Alberta-British Columbia gas or else permitting us to build an auxiliary line into that area to augment the supply from New Mexico. If this attempt fails, then a conference should be called of the provincial governments concerned and the federal government, as well as the authorities who are in charge of investing large sums of money with a view to building the gas line from the Peace river country into the lower mainland of British Columbia.
I have considerable information on this project. I might point out to the minister that as late as April 12 or 13, 1954, a three-day conference was held at Portland by the Pacific northwest trade association. All delegates attending that conference were very anxious to have the gas line run from the Peace river country into the lower regions of British Columbia and on into the states of Washington, Oregon, and down into northern California. If the minister is not aware of it, and I am quite sure he must be, the membership of this particular group reads like who's who in the business world. There were 32 members from trade or gas companies, the British Columbia electric, and so on, from Vancouver; 23 members from Portland, Oregon; 50 members from the city of Seattle; 20 members from the city of Spokane; and there was a supplementary list of upwards of 150 or 200 delegates, all of whom are industrialists in the Pacific northwest.

Their resolution No. 11 had to do with the extension of the line, and reads as follows:

I consider that a very important resolution in view of the fact that it was passed at that meeting. The resolution, which was passed practically unanimously, was endorsed by the Northwest Pipe Coating Corporation, the Seattle Gas Company, Puget Power Company, Boeing Aeroplane Company, Pacific Power and Light Company, Portland Chamber of Commerce, Portland Gas and Coke Company and the Eugene Water and Electric Board.
You will note that practically all the firms having to do with power in the Pacific northwest, including our own from British Columbia, were very interested in having this gas legislation passed as proposed.
Now, I would not go as far as the Vancouver Sun has gone in its editorial of June 19 of this year, in suggesting reprisal action; but I think that sometimes it is necessary to suggest what action we might take to reciprocate in respect of their thoughtless treatment of our request that gas be piped into the northwestern United States. On the point the Sun has this to say:
Ottawa must demand immediate reconsideration by top U.S. administrators of the perverse ban clamped on B.C. natural gas entering Washington and Oregon by the U.S. federal power commission. Our government should bluntly remind Washington, D.C., that Canada could, play at economic nationalism to great U.S. disadvantage.
Ottawa could point out that B.C. is in no mood to harness its Columbia river water to supply desperately needed hydroelectric power to the U.S. northwest when FPC can't trust us to serve gas consumers fairly in the same area.
I would like to remind this government, particularly the minister now before the committee-because he was minister at that time-that when the Anaconda mine required a large supply of natural gas there was no question of the fact that Alberta could supply the gas in the quantities required. Nor was there any suggestion at any time that the supplier might be unreliable. At the time the request was made to supply the Anaconda mine in the United States with gas, that line was built and the export permit was given.
