Supply-Defence Production There has been no difficulty in so far as the shipments of gas are concerned into that part of the United States.
The transportation of gas is so important in the defence set-up of the Pacific northwest that, if we are going to try to keep our industries in operation, it is important that this exchange be continued. As I said earlier, I would not go so far as to suggest that what the Vancouver Sun suggests by way of reprisal should be endorsed by parliament. However, I think it should be drawn to the attention of the United States authorities that the two of us can very handily play at the same game.
The following is a press report which has since been substantiated by the fact that we could not send our gas into the United States. The following appears in the Vancouver Province of June 19, and refers to one of the larger consumers of the product in Portland. The press article says:
Charles Gueffroy, president of Portland Gas and Coke Company, Portland, Oregon, biggest potential customer, said his company will not sign anything but a "pay as we use at an agreed price" contract with Pacific Northwest, the winning pipeline. "Without our contract I doubt if Pacific can get financial backing," he said.
Mr. Gueffroy said the decision "injected unfortunate international aspects and I predict that even the White House will take note of it."
It can be seen from this one large consumer just how essential it is that a gas line should be built. I know our minister is well aware of the situation. He is aware of the fact that it is very necessary to the people of British Columbia, if we are to carry on the industrial development we have been expecting to carry on. I believe he knows of the development that is taking place in my own riding, where some $70 million is being invested by a British syndicate looking after the estate of the Duke of Westminster. That site alone will probably account for some 80,000 families in that riding in the not too distant future, when the ultimate goal of complete industrialization is reached.
The matter, of course, has to do entirely with policy. And I come back to that, because I feel that to a certain degree our government has been neglectful of letting our policy be made known to the Americans, particularly when they expect us to help them. When they expect that, then naturally we expect that they will give some help to us. This matter of trade, whether in connection with gas for defence purposes, or for any other purpose, is a very far-reaching one. A policy whereby we allow Texas gas to enter the Niagara peninsula for only five years might well have its effect upon the


Pacific Northwest decision made by the commission, because we have given our approval to bringing gas into that area.
By the same token I think we should expect further consideration from the proper authorities in the United States, when we bring to their attention the far-reaching effects on our defence production alone, if for no other reason. The same is true of the United States. We should bring to their attention the far-reaching consequences of this matter on our defence production alone if for no other reason than that the safety of the United States and of Canada might well depend upon this gas.
The hon. member for one of the Kootenay ridings mentioned the other day the steel industry that he hoped would be built in his riding. Certainly, anyone who knows the worth of steel and the fact that coke and coal are found in the region, together with gas, which could be supplied to that region, knows that it would be a tremendous boon to that area. It is more essential to bring this about now than ever before. I request the minister to try to get in touch with the proper authorities in the United States with a view to getting them to change their decision in respect of bringing gas into the northwestern United States. Let us build our line. If that is impossible, then give us the assurance that the United States people will use our gas to supplement their own. If that is not done, then the third proposal should be undertaken. We should go ahead and build a gas line from the Peace river country into the Vancouver market with the help of Canadian industrialists and investments by the public, as well as the help of the government of British Columbia.

On Saturday last I asked the Minister of Defence Production a question with regard to this decision which has been made by the United States federal power commission, and he gave a satisfactory reply. I realize the minister is just as much concerned about overcoming this difficulty as are those of us who represent constituencies in British Columbia.
Since Saturday I have had an opportunity to read the west coast press and I think I can say without exaggeration that there is great concern, great worry there over this situation. In any event, I have never seen the press upset so quickly as they have been over this particular decision. As the minister knows, the opening up of the Peace river district of British Columbia and Alberta is dependent to a very large extent on the possibility of exporting the gas. If no way is

found by which that gas can be got to market, then the development of that northern portion of Canada will be delayed for a generation. That will be particularly tragic, because much of our danger comes from the north. If there ever were an attack on this country it would come from Siberia or over the pole, and that northern country is of the utmost importance from a strategic point of view as well as in many other ways.
As far as British Columbia is concerned, there has been a great deal of publicity about natural gas being available. That publicity has been going on for several years, and to a remarkable degree the people have the idea that the economic development of the province depends to quite a large extent on getting gas from the Peace river. It is felt there that every part of the province would benefit; of course the central part of the province would, including such centres as Prince George and Kamloops. Then, there is the Okanagan valley and the Kootenay country where the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company is located at Trail. That company would be as large a consumer of natural gas as greater Vancouver. Down in the lower mainland of the province the British Columbia Electric Railway Company has been planning to use this gas, and many schemes have been on the drawing board which are based on the use of Peace river gas.
I believe it would also be possible to pipe the gas over to Vancouver island, and there it would be a fine source of power. They have not too much electric power there, and the natural gas would be of great benefit.
I notice in the press that the former premier of British Columbia, the Hon. Byron Johnson, said that he had in mind the provincial government taking part financially in the construction of this natural gas pipe line from the Peace river, in the event of the decision of the United States federal power commission being unfavourable.
I had not realized that before, but I think that he had planned to provide over half the capital for the construction of such a line. The present provincial government is very deeply committed to the project. I fancy that it too would be willing to help in the construction of a line.
I believe that if a line were built now it would not be very long before the Americans would be scrambling to get the gas. It could be finished before the line from the San Juan basin comes through, and apparently the reserves in that area of the United States are not very extensive. I was given that impression by a statement made by one of the 83276-408
Supply-Defence Production directors of the Westcoast Transmission Company as reported in the Vancouver Province of June 18. I refer to Norman Whittall. He had this to say:
If Canada "goes it alone" on the natural gas pipeline from the Peace river, the United States will ask to come in, said Norman R. Whittall, one of the chief figures in Westcoast Transmission Company's battle for the line.
"We should build a 24-inch gas line to Vancouver, irrespective of anything else," he commented when informed of today's turndown by the United States federal power commission.
I believe the original plan was to put in a 24-inch line. The article continues:
The citizens of British Columbia should support the project and the government should guarantee the bonds. It is only a matter of time until there will be so much pressure from an educated American public that federal power commission will be forced to upset its ruling. Gas reserves of the Pacific Northwest Pipeline Corporation are not sufficient to supply the potential market in the Pacific northwest area of the United States."
I believe the main objective now is to see that the construction of a pipe line is not unduly delayed. It would be vital for defence production on the west coast as well as being vital for the development of the north country and of the province as a whole. I realize that on Saturday the minister said he would do everything he could to help get this situation remedied, but I have been wondering whether a project of this kind would qualify for capital assistance under the minister's department. It may be that such would not be the case, but I ask the minister whether he would be willing to have a complete investigation made of the situation just as soon as possible after the house rises. I know I do not need to ask for his assurance that he will do everything within his power to see that this project goes ahead.
We have lost the first battle, but we have not lost the war. I believe this scheme is so important to the future of Canada that some means should be found of bringing about the construction of the line through co-operation of the people interested and of the provincial government; and whatever help can be given by the dominion government should be made available. Could the minister say whether this would be a project which could be made eligible for capital assistance under the vote in his department?

Mr. Chairman, it does not come under any of the rules governing capital assistance about which I know.
I might say that the policy for the sale of western gas is made in the west and not,
I am sorry to say, in Ottawa, because I think we might do a little better. There has always been a theory advanced that the best market

Supply-Defence Production for western gas is in the United States, and a great exponent of that theory is the hon. member for Calgary South. I believe his views are shared by the premier of Alberta. That theory is that all we have to do is to deliver the gas across the international boundary and it would be snapped up immediately. I have thought for a long time that the sponsors of this project were taking rather a long shot in attempting to serve that particular market by gas from the Peace river area. I felt that the other applicants who proposed to take the gas from southern Alberta should have received more consideration than they were given in this house. I remember that my hon. friend himself led a filibuster during two sessions of parliament to prevent those proposals receiving consideration in this house. I felt that a supply from southern Alberta would have had a much better chance of entering that market rather than a pipe line from northern Alberta. All I can say for this government is that we have done everything we possibly could to see that western gas was made available and done all we could to help the marketing of that gas. I believe in doing everything to develop our economy and the use of our natural resources to the best advantage. I have long maintained that the best market for Alberta's gas is in Canada, and that the greatest contribution that gas could make to the economy of any part of the country is to find markets for it in Canada. That is what we are attempting to do.
I would point out that we had to wait two years after the first application for export to the United States was granted before we could get permission to export gas to eastern Canada. We obtained that permit during the last two or three months and that is a project to which I think the government can give some assistance. As both projects were started by others and controlled by others, and for which the permits are given by others it has been very difficult for this government to get a toehold to an extent that we could be really useful.
I think I am as interested as anyone else in making sure that Canada develops to the fullest extent possible using all her natural resources, and I am very sorry indeed that that gas in the Peace river area is going to be tied up for some time at least. However, I think the decision to bring in gas from the San Juan basin is only a temporary hold-up because I believe there is not enough gas in that area to supply the domestic users and there is nothing available for industry. I presume there will in time be a demand for northern gas if it is then available, but the difference is that the franchise for the area has been given to the United States company


and I presume the Canadian company will be required to deal with that company rather than deal directly with the consumers, which I think will be unfortunate.
Is it a fact that the bulk of the gas in the Peace river district is in British Columbia and not in Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I think the larger quantity of the gas as committed to this particular project lies in Alberta, but a good part of it lies in British Columbia, and I dare say more drilling would disclose more gas in British Columbia. I therefore think it would be correct to say that the supply is in both provinces.

When we asked the minister about this matter the other day he said that there would be no obstacle at this end in the way of making arrangements between west gas and the Pacific Northwest company. I just wish to briefly support what has been said here by the previous speakers as to the importance to the development of our province of finding an outlet for this gas, and I should like to ask the minister whether I am correct in my understanding that up to the present time it has always been considered that the logical outlet for Peace river gas was the Pacific northwest. Can he tell me if that is still the case? While I know we cannot say whether a private company will make a deal with another private company, and certainly there is no way in which we can or should compel them to do so, is it not obvious and logical, when you have gas bursting the wells-I do not want to exaggerate it-and we are told the Pacific northwest area of the United States has a growth potential considerably in excess of that which can be supplied from the San Juan fields, that such an arrangement would be a practical and desirable one, and that the two companies should get together and work out an arrangement for a supply fitting into the grid for which the United States company now has the franchise to put in available Peace river gas so that the demands of that area would be met and the gas come down through our province? It seems to me the interest of both countries would then be met, and the potential shortage of gas in the Pacific northwest would be supplemented by gas from the Peace river area. The interests of British Columbia as an entity would also be served. I do not want to ask the minister to be a prophet, but I would be interested in knowing whether that strikes him as a logical and desirable plan.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not think I should comment as to what would be logical and desirable. The Westcoast Transmission Company has an export permit for a certain quantity of gas from that area and certainly this government will take no action to interfere in any arrangement that may be found possible to provide for the disposal of that gas in the United States. But I might add that I am not sufficiently familiar with all the facts and therefore I do not like to comment.

Supply-Defence Production "that time was done on behalf of the government by dollar-a-year men. They were men who were taken in from the large industries across Canada. It is only natural-it is only human nature-that, if an official is in a position of spending the taxpayers' money for the purpose of expanding an industry, creating an industry or selling a commodity, he is going to think of his own plant or firm. I think that was the main reason why you had during the war in the centre of the country a lop-sided development in our industrial creations.
In the spending of the $2 billion that is indicated in these estimates for the creation of industry and for defence purchasing these officers or men in positions of direction at this time-in every field, from the legal fraternity down to the economist, the consultant and the contract expert-are all on loan from some industry, I presume, from the centre of Canada. Before consideration of his estimates is concluded, the minister can tell us who make up that personnel and where they come from. In my judgment it is personnel of that kind who are not particular as to how the economy is protected or what kind of development takes place as long as the firm or plant for which they work is looked after. They are not in here for nothing. They do not live for nothing. Someone is paying their salaries. The someone they are thinking of and working for is the someone who is paying their salaries. I am reasonably sure that not many of these directors, consultants, legal advisers and contract experts came in here from Nova Scotia-

-with the exception, of course, of the minister's parliamentary assistant; and of course he is only one man and it is rather difficult for him to watch the whole crowd. I hope it will continue because, as I said previously, this could be a good nucleus of a planning commission that could take under consideration many of the problems that are created today because sufficient thinking has not been done about them.
Again, at page 38 of the minister's report there is another item that provokes my thought and supports exactly what I was saying a few moments ago. At page 38 of the minister's report there is a section with

the caption "Small Industries Division" and at the bottom of the page there is this paragraph:
Much of the educational and liaison work of the division was completed during the year, as most companies interested in securing defence orders had made their facilities known and understood the policies and procedures followed by the department. As a result, the district offices were closed down at the end of the year and the Ottawa staff was reduced to two industry relations officers.
That suggests to me that the dollar a year men of the big industries, or those fellows who were working for nothing, were quite satisfied in planning the work of the department that there was no need of small industries in this country, that the big ones could take care of everything and if they were not big enough they could be expanded. There are many parts of this country where small industry is not only needed but the economy is in desperate straits because industries are dying. The report of the department says that they have been turning out all kinds of guns, machine tools and other equipment for the NATO countries. That equipment goes to Europe. The shortest route to Europe is from Sydney, Nova Scotia. There is a huge steel plant there. I have never been able to understand why, under such a set-up as that of the minister's department, some of the materials for the NATO countries are not manufactured in that part of the country where the raw steel, iron ore and labour are available.
It is right at tidewater. I never could understand why these things are manufactured in central Canada and dragged all the way across the country to be shipped instead of being manufactured in that part of the country and shipped from there. As I said when I began, with a little bit of selfishness and the geographical difficulties and the difficulties created by the British North America Act, you have got a pretty tough combination. I think it is that little bit of selfishness that keeps everything centralized in Ontario and Quebec because logically and economically the place to manufacture and ship equipment for the NATO countries is in the maritime provinces.
I can understand risk capital not going in there, but I cannot understand a department like the minister's, which is investing the taxpayers' money, placing industry that is going to turn out that kind of equipment in the most illogical part of the country where the products have to be dragged across the country to the sea to be shipped. In many cases the raw material is taken from that part of the country, processed in the central provinces and the finished products are then transported to Halifax, Montreal or Sydney

to be shipped. I am pretty sure that if the minister were doing that kind of planning for himself it would not be done that way.
But I am afraid that much of the planning, as I said before, is done by people who are interested in maintaining the kind of set-up we have in Canada today, with centralization of everything in the two central provinces. Let me give the minister two examples of the attitude: "We are not particular what happens in other parts of the country as long as we are selling our own commodity". I asked the Minister of National Defence a question yesterday with respect to the large naval base at Sydney, Nova Scotia. There is a steel plant within half a mile of the base, and at that steel plant there is a large wire and nail mill. At the present time at least 50 per cent of the people usually employed in that nail mill are unemployed. Why are nails dragged from Hamilton, Ontario, for use on that naval base at Sydney, Nova Scotia? Why could they not have been bought half a mile away? They could have been purchased more cheaply because you would not have the freight rate to pay for the long haul from Hamilton to Sydney.
That is merely an example but it is a very pertinent one; because, if that is what goes on with respect to a small purchase like that what takes place when the contract runs into millions of dollars?
The second example I wish to bring to the minister's attention has to do with the heating of national defence buildings. I have a couple of their requisition forms in my hand. The armouries at Sackville, New Brunswick, are located within a few miles of the coal mines at Springhill, Nova Scotia. Up until 1953 these armouries were heated by coal purchased from the Springhill area at a cost of $16.50 a ton.
When the contract was sent out in 1953 the dealer in Moncton, New Brunswick, who supplied the coal was told that in the future he had to supply anthracite coal from the United States. He wrote and said that it was rather difficult, that he would have to bring it in in small lots and it would be difficult to handle it in that way. Do not forget that the use of anthracite coal increased the cost of heating the building over 100 per cent. It cost $35 a ton while the other cost $16.50 a ton. But that switch was made. I should like to ask the minister if the person who prepared that form and sent it out was not more interested in promoting the sale of United States coal than he was in maintaining some market for an industry that was in very serious economic difficulties at the time.
These are only two examples, nails and coal, and these things took place in a section
Supply-Defence Production of the country where, as the minister knows, unemployment is perhaps more serious than in any other part of Canada. Both the provincial government and the people of the province have pointed out that they face a crisis that is beyond their control, but even with respect to such small items that part of the country was ignored and forgotten. In the light of these two small examples, I am; reasonably sure that the same thinking runs through all the planning of the purchasing of defence requirements, the letting of contracts and so forth.	,
I am not saying this by way of criticism. I am bringing it to the minister's attention now because there is a lot of money still to be spent on national defence, and national defence is going to last as long as we last. One of the best means of civil defence that I know of today is to try to get those who are planning our defence production requirements to think in terms of not putting all our eggs in one basket and concentrating practically all our production in eastern Ontario where it can be knocked out with one bomb. What I have suggested is in my opinion one of the best means of civil defence that I can think of at the present time. In addition, it would at least mean a livelihood to people in sections of Canada which are at the crossroads today unless something is done.
I am not going to say any more. I want the minister to do some thinking about this matter because I am convinced that men do not enter the service of the government from Canada Packers, National Steel or any of. these other industries for nothing. There is remuneration somewhere. They are working for somebody who is paying their salaries, and their planning will be done in accordance with the best interests of the people who are paying their wages.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I think I should reply to this immediately. I am disappointed in my hon. friend. I have heard him make some very able and fair-minded speeches in the nineteen years we have sat in the House of Commons. I can hardly believe that he thinks that people offer their services and their services are being accepted with the sole thought that they will promote the interests of their own particular business. That is the statement he has just made. In the first place people do not offer their services. We have to go out and find them, make arrangements with their companies and beg them to come here. In the second place, never in all my experience with men borrowed from industry have I known these men to help their own industries deliberately. In fact they usually lean backward. If there

Supply-Defence Production is not enough business to go around in the industry, they usually say: Fill the others up and our people will do the best they can. That has been the attitude in my experience. My hon. friend has suggested the only reason the maritime provinces are not full of defence plants is that we have selfish people in Ottawa who prevented the plants going there.
Let us analyse that statement. When we find something to be manufactured, we first look to existing industry to carry out that operation. The only reason that we sponsor new building at all is that existing industry has not sufficient capacity to produce what is required. You say, if the industry has not enough productive capacity, why not move a plant to Nova Scotia and build there? The difficulty is that it requires some specialized skill to be able to produce most things that are in short supply. In the first place, someone must know the kind of plant that is required, the kind of equipment that is required, and must have the nucleus of an organization. At least, they must have skilled and experienced engineers, operators skilled in management of that particular enterprise, then they must draw on a nucleus of skilled labour in the area. You cannot attract that kind of labour from one area to an area where the workers have every reason to believe the plant cannot exist under highly competitive conditions.
You have those factors to consider. I suggest we have not neglected the maritimes, and have taken there all the industries we could take. I will tell the hon. member one of the worst mistakes I ever made in planning industry was to put up $5 million to help in the construction of a plate mill at Sydney. This plate mill operated for two or three months, and when the war was over it was broken up and dispersed; that was the last of the plate mill and the last of the government's $5 million. It is quite useless to establish industries to do a war job that cannot exist under normal conditions. It does not do the district any good. True, it provides employment for a short time, and spreads around some money for a short time. But the fact the plant is standing there idle does more harm to the area than if the project had never been started.
What have we been able to do for the maritimes? I am rather proud of the fact I persuaded an English aircraft manufacturer to establish himself in Halifax. Our Canadian manufacturers were not willing to do that. We had tried to get several of them to consider establishing an aircraft plant at Halifax. However, when the Fairey Aviation Company came out, I happened to see


them before anyone else did. I particularly asked them to take a good look at Halifax, because I thought they could do very well there. They did that, and as my hon. friend knows, that company has established a very substantial industry in Nova Scotia.
We had an opportunity to help establish an electronics industry in the maritimes, too, but that is not doing so well. It has created considerable employment, and I am very hopeful that it can survive during normal times. The hon. member has talked about a shipyard in Cape Breton. I do not remember any shipyard in Cape Breton before the Department of Defence Production started to function.
It is a naval base.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
A naval base; nevertheless it was built by the Department of Defence Production. I hope it will be a substantial industry. The Ferguson shipyards are there, but that is a small operation except for the contracts from the Department of Defence Production. Amherst has a substantial industry. We kept that industry busy when the department of munitions and supply was functioning, but when the department went out of business, the industry closed down. When the Department of Defence Production started to function, the industry opened up and is now a substantial employer of men. I think if the hon. member will look around Nova Scotia, he will find that the department has supported existing industry and has brought in any industry willing to go to the maritimes and capable of surviving after military requirements had been provided for.
When it is suggested that the men in the department here tried to locate those industries somewhere else, I assure the hon. member that if they had not worked to establish industry in the maritimes, none of these industries would have been in Nova Scotia today. It has taken the loyal cooperation of every man in the Department of Defence Production to see that those industries were located there and to see that they have been brought to the state of prosperity they are enjoying today.
The hon. member has spoken of two examples of malfeasance, if you like, on the part of the department. One concerns these nails. I should like to know how many nails? Did the hon. member count the kegs? The fact of the matter is that nails are sold everywhere. We have a nail plant in Sydney, Cape Breton; we have a nail plant in Hamilton and we have a nail plant in Vancouver. I can assure him that Sydney nails are sold in Vancouver, and

I have every reason to believe that Sydney nails are sold in Hamilton. I am certain the Steel Company of Canada offer nails for sale in Sydney and in Vancouver as well. I do not believe the Vancouver plant reaches down that far because it is a small operation, not associated with a primary producer.
These nails are undoubtedly on sale in hardware stores. A man might have needed a keg of nails, and while waiting for a shipment may have gone into a hardware store and bought a keg of nails without paying too much attention to the label on the barrel. They might have been shipped out of naval stores and routed in there incorrectly. It is the policy of the department not only to pay slightly more for products coming from the maritime areas or provinces not having substantial industry, but to go to some trouble to try to build up those areas. It is our policy, on an even break, to always buy from the operation nearest to the consuming plant. I should like to know more about those nails. I have asked our general purchasing department, but they can find no trace of any order of Hamilton nails for Sydney.
I saw them.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: How many did you see?
I have seen ten or fifteen kegs.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That may be a lot
of nails in that particular operation, but it is not a great many nails. I suppose they are worth about $5 a keg, something like that, and that would be $75 worth of nails.
Then the hon. member spoke about coal at Sackville. He has been told about that. We get the specifications from the Department of National Defence. It is the privilege of that department to write the specifications for what they require, and our department purchases as requested. The specifications came over calling for anthracite coal for that particular armoury. They were processed through the department. I think these specifications should have been called to someone's attention. The complaints came in, and it was called to the attention of the Department of National Defence. They admitted the mistake, and the next coal that is ordered there will, of course, be local coal. I presume when you are buying a billion dollars worth of supplies a year, mistakes will happen. I have been rather happy they have not been great in number, but that was undoubtedly a mistake which is being corrected.

I am glad that I deliberately made my talk provocative.

There is one thing I want to tell the minister. You can find skilled personnel in that area for any plant you wish to establish. In so far as the plate mill is concerned, that mill was built twice. I am not blaming the federal government for all the disabilities of Nova Scotia, because in my judgment the provincial government is about 50 per cent responsible. The other 50 per cent could be shared between the federal government and Dominion Steel and Coal company.
That mill was built twice, you know. It was built in the first war at a cost of $11 million, and never produced a thing. Then, all the machinery from the mill disappeared. At that time we were importing 90 per cent of our steel plate from the United States. Why Dosco did not maintain that mill is not hard to understand. They have a mill somewhere else; and you subsidize the raw material coming up.

I wonder if I might ask the minister a very simple question. The answer may not be quite as simple as the question. I am wondering where the minister's department, the Department of Defence suggest this has nothing to do with the Department of National Defence in the location and building of various defence projects.
My question is based upon a telegram received this morning from the hon. member for Cariboo. This telegram was sent to the hon. member for Peace River, the leader of this group, and is as follows:
Could you ask ministry in view of prospective transfer of R.C.A.F. western headquarters from Vancouver and strategic importance of Prince George in northern defences, will ministry say whether consideration will be given to transferring headquarters to Prince George. Is ministry aware of advantages of Prince George airport?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That of course is a matter entirely for the Department of National Defence, as to where it has its headquarters. As far as procurement goes, it is the function of the Department of National Defence to say what it wants, furnish the specification, determine the place of delivery and the time of delivery, and to make the money available by a financial encumbrance. After that it is the function of the Department of Defence Production to determine how the material will be procured and where it will be procured, and all factors of that kind.
The proper procedure then is to call this matter to the attention of the Minister of National Defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.

I was interested this morning to hear the minister announce that it is his intention to place the Department of Defence Production on a more permanent basis. Its activities have assumed such proportions now that this development is very important and necessary. I know it will bring much satisfaction to the aircraft industry especially which has been uncertain as to its future in the economy of this country. At the same time I was disappointed a few months ago to learn that the small defence industries branch of the department was winding up its affairs. It is this particular aspect of the departmental activities that I wish to say something about this afternoon.
Supply-Defence Production
Is this branch of the department winding up its affairs because it is felt that its program has been completed, or does the reason arise from the fact that the Department of Defence Production has found it is impossible to work out the original purpose of the small defence industries branch? I have the feeling that the latter reason must be the one because, as I said, the small defence industries branch was initiated to assist in the work of decentralization of defence industries. We have had several dissertations on this theme during the discussion today and no doubt there will be more before we wind up our discussion this afternoon. As I see the effects of the operation of the small defence industries branch, I cannot come to the conclusion that it has had the desired effect, at least in my part of the country, that was originally intended. I would appreciate very much if the minister could indicate why it has been decided to discontinue the work of this important branch.
I sometimes wonder if the minister has come under the influence of the myth that so far as industrial development is concerned the west is catching up with the east. That is an idea that is very frequently put forward even in well-informed circles of this country. In fact I have even heard it from some of my fellow members from the province of Manitoba.
During the budget debate I referred to some statistics which indicated that the reverse was the fact. That is, that rather than catching up, the western provinces are actually going farther behind. The boom that they are enjoying, in comparison to the economic boom in Ontario and Quebec, is a relatively minor one. On June 18 I received a parliamentary return which brings these figures up to 1953, and I note the same trends are continued. I asked for the statistics of total new investment in manufacturing, the number of new post-war manufacturing plants and the employment resulting from the establishment of those plants as well as the total production figures, and I see that in each case the trends are strongly in favour of the large central provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
In view of the fact that I have had several members ask to see these statistics, I am wondering whether I can get the permission of the committee to have them placed on the record.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What are they?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

The point I was making, and I think perhaps the hon. member for Eglinton outlined it quite succinctly, is that there is no basis of truth at all in the idea that the western provinces as well as the maritime provinces are catching up or even keeping pace with the industrial development in the central provinces. The reason why I bring this matter into a discussion on the defence production estimates is that I think the minister has succumbed to the myth himself. Speaking in Winnipeg last spring before the chamber of commerce the minister took issue with members of parliament from the west who were constantly decrying the industrial development situation in Canada and pointing out that there was a continuing imbalance. By that statement he implied, I believe, that things were not as bad as they had been in the west, and that any western member who took that attitude was promoting bad public relations for the district he represented.
The same opinion has been expressed by Dr. Firestone, of the Department of Trade and Commerce, when he said in an address before the trade and industry officials of the ten provincial governments that there were no longer any "have-not" provinces in Canada, and that every one of them was a "have". He added, and I quote him directly:
True, some provinces have more of one thing than another, but every province has found that it has *a good deal of natural resources that can be put to good use with hard work, drive, vision and the proverbial good luck. In other words, the opportunities are there-it is a question of grasping them.
I agree broadly with his idea, but the truth is that, so far as the actual situation in Canada is concerned, those words are still in the realm of prophecy. The very fact that this house clings so tenaciously to tax rental agreements indicates that we recognize the principle that there are certain areas in this country that need additional support because they occupy an unfavourable economic and financial position. Every time redistribution comes up for discussion in this house it is the west which suffers in terms of representation here, and that representation is on a-

The whole basis for my remarks, Mr. Chairman, is the discontinuance of the small industries branch of this defence department. As I said in my opening remarks, I cannot imagine that this branch of the department has been discontinued because it has completed its work. I feel it has been discontinued because it has been found impossible, due to overwhelming economic and political pressure from the central provinces, for the small defence industries branch to carry out the original purpose for which it was established. In supporting that contention I have pointed out that a situation still exists in these underdeveloped areas of Canada, if I may use that phrase, which demands the continued operation of the work of this department. I cannot imagine anything which could be more closely related to the subject matter now under discussion.
We in the western provinces, and certainly in Manitoba, are not interested in handouts. That has tended to be the policy of the central government for years when we get into economic difficulties during a depression or as indicated by the tax rental agreements. We want an expression of confidence in our future from this government here at Ottawa. I believe that the tremendous sums involved in expenditures by the Department of Defence Production have provided a golden opportunity for the dominion government to assist in overcoming some of these historical trends, the pressure from the central provinces, which produce such an uneven development in other parts of the country.
Our provincial government in Manitoba is beginning to cope with the problem on the local level. Our minister of resources and
6466	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production development has been making contacts in the United States and in the United Kingdom in order to help to overcome the problem so far as possible on the provincial level. However, I say that if we are going to compete successfully with the tremendous social power that is generated by the concentration of population in this central part of Canada, the federal government should seize every possible opportunity for a more equitable distribution of industry.
In concluding, Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister why the small defence industry activity has been discontinued.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will refer to the report of the Department of Defence Production for the year 1953 he will find the answer. Under the heading "Small Industries Division", the report sets out the function of the division and the section finishes with this paragraph:
Much of the educational and liaison work of the division was completed during the year, as most companies interested in securing defence orders had made their facilities known and understood the policies and procedures followed by the department. As a result, the district offices were closed down at the end of the year and the Ottawa staff was reduced to two industry relations officers.
In other words, the work is being done; but in an effort to promote economy we did hot believe it was worth while to carry ten branch offices in the provinces when the work left to be done was not sufficient to keep them busy. We have therefore concentrated the work in Ottawa in the person of two industry relations officers. I think that nowhere is there to be found a better example of the work of the small industries division than is to be found in the work in the Winnipeg area. If you will talk to the small manufacturers there, I think they will tell you that they are doing government work because they were introduced to the work by the small industries division. They know their way around now and they do not need anyone to hold their hands. That is the situation all across Canada. The small manufacturer as well as the large manufacturer understands the work or the function of the department.
I might point out to my hon. friend that since this department was formed in 1951, it has placed orders in the number of 386,585. If he thinks that all those orders have been placed with big business, he could not be more wrong. I think that far more of them have been placed with businesses with a capitalization under $100,000 than have been placed with businesses with a capitalization of more than that.

Mr. Chairman, I just wish to speak briefly again. The fact that the minister mentioned the Winnipeg area does not deal with the problem I was raising because Winnipeg is a large metropolitan community with a very healthy economic base. In fact most of the industrial development that has taken place in the province of Manitoba since the war has taken place in that area which has almost half of our population resources. In Manitoba we are cursed with double centralization, namely centralization in the east and this centralization in one large urban area. The latest statistics I have indicate that 85 per cent of new industries have developed within the greater Winnipeg area.
Let me carry this matter just one stage further. One of the reasons why I emphasize the role of the defence production department in this matter of decentralization is that the work is directly connected with defence and, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South pointed out, it is only good defence planning to carry out as comprehensive as possible dispersal of defence potential. I listened carefully to the minister when he made his statement this morning dealing with the aircraft industry. He referred to the widespread dispersal of the aircraft industry, particularly that part of the industry dealing with the manufacturing of component parts, and he mentioned mostly large urban areas. I did not hear one small centre mentioned. There was Halifax, Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg, Calgary, Vancouver and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: And Amherst, Nova Scotia.
Yes; and Amherst.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
St. Jean, Quebec and
Edmonton.

Let us look at the Russian program in contrast to our own. They have 360 factories engaged in the manufacturing of aircraft and the component parts thereof. I have obtained that information from Jane's "All the World's Aircraft" which is supposed to be a very reliable document on these matters. Of these 360 factories, 35 are airframe factories, 30 are aero-engine factories and 265 are producing the other smaller components. They are dispersed just as widely as possible throughout the expansive geographic area of the U.S.S.R. In addition to general dispersal they are concentrating on northern development with regard to their industrial activity and they have above the 53rd parallel 50 cities which have been established on an industrial base. We have just

one city north of the 53rd parallel. The point I wish to make is that we should not contribute to bigness and the overdevelopment of these metropolitan areas but try to support in every way possible the development of small industries in smaller communities. That is real decentralization. The small industry in the small community is able to cope successfully with the larger industrial plants in most circumstances, but certainly it cannot do so when it comes to manufacturing activities that are closely integrated with our whole defence program.
If it was not for private activities in this regard, there would be little industrial development at all in Manitoba at the present time because the degree of prosperity and progress that we have, particularly in the western section of the province, is based on the oil activity that has emerged during the past three years. As the minister well knows, that activity is largely in the hands of private operators. Again I would emphasize not concentration in Winnipeg or in the larger urban areas but support wherever possible in the small communities. It seems to me that is the main purpose for the establishment of this small industries division.

In the course of my remarks on the first item this morning the minister took exception to my referring to the original estimate of the cost of minesweepers as a target price. He insisted that it was merely an estimate and objected to my use of the term "target price". I should like to see if we can get some information with regard to the cost of these vessels since I understand that one of them has now been completed on the west coast. I would refer the minister to page 539 of Hansard of December 2, 1953, when I attempted last to elicit some information from the government on the cost of these projects. At that time I asked this question of the government:
1.	What were the prices originally set for the construction of minesweepers which were under construction in shipyards in eastern Canada and British Columbia in the years 1951, 1952 and 1953?
2.	Were these prices increased?
3.	If so, when, and by how much?
4.	What were the reasons for the increases?
5.	What is the contract price for the most recent contracts let for the construction of minesweepers?
You will observe that the minister placed an answer on Hansard to the effect that all that had been done at that time was to make an estimate of probable costs. He tells us that contracts were awarded providing for payment to the contractors of up
Supply-Defence Production to $925,000 per vessel and that additional sums have been authorized from time to time against which payments have been made' to the contractors. The rest of my question he dismisses as not applicable.
If we grant that it was not possible for the government to get a closer estimate at that time, I think now is the time that we should have some more figures. speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am sorry to say that I have not with me the exact cost of the ten minesweepers that have been completed, but it is slightly under $4 million per minesweeper. It varies for the different yards. I think the lowest cost yard happens to be at Port Arthur, Ontario, with which I am very pleased, and some of the higher costs are found in one or two of the yards the hon. member has mentioned. However, I think they are all being bought for slightly under $4 million. That is exclusive of armament, fire control equipment and stores.
When a requisition comes from the Department of National Defence for a new type of ship, it is accompanied by an estimate. The estimate is made by the man who proposes to design the ship. We have no way of knowing what the ship is going to look like when it is designed. The design is perhaps
6468	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production finished a year or so later. We accept the estimate. As the designs go forward we try to estimate what the position is from time to time, but design changes are made almost up until the date of commissioning. The work is carried out on a basis of cost plus a fee. The cost is just what the yard finds it necessary under supervision to spend on the building of the ship. We believe we now know sufficient about the cost of a minesweeper to set up a target price. In fixing a target price say we find that the lowest cost ship built is $31 million. We consider that with their past experience they should do a bit better in the future and we set the target at $3J million. If the final price is less than that, the shipyard gets a bonus. If it costs more than the target, the shipyard fee is cut accordingly. That is a target price contract, and it is fixed on a price that is sufficiently well known to be established and agreed upon as fair by the crown and the contractor.

I should like to say a few words on the problem of decentralization and good planning for the future. I find myself in agreement to quite an extent with the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Cape Breton South. If nothing has been done, which I would not be too surprised to learn, possibly he might give us a reason for it. It might be a different reason from what I suspect he may say, namely, that there is a shortage of power there.
I think this department will have a great deal to do in the future with the over-all picture of planning for the defence of this country and in my opinion the department should expand their thinking and plan to assist these areas. If they do not have existing industries today it might be good business to help industries to get started thereby assisting in the development of natural resources such as power. speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am surprised that the hon. member for Yictoria-Carleton has not noticed the fairly substantial industry being built there at the present time. At least $30 million is being spent on the army camp at Gagetown which will be a continuing industry for that part of the country and one that will absorb local products in a way that no other industry I can think of would equal. I know that there is one on the north shore at Bathurst that is doing an excellent job for the department. In order to help someone you must find the person to help, and the person who wants help must indicate he wants help. He must indicate what he is capable of doing. Wherever we find that type of person or that type of industry in New Brunswick or anywhere else, we give them help. I suggest that Mr. Hesler of Sackville might be able to tell my hon. friend about the help he has had from the crown in developing industry there and in Nova Scotia.
I do not believe I could give a catalogue of all the industries that have been developed in New Brunswick. The minister's estimates are not so easy to discuss. speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: In order to do that we would have to analyse how much Dosco steel went into our construction and how much the basic industries down there supplied to us. Oh, yes. There was an investment in Dosco for the new press I mentioned that was installed there; that must have run into several million dollars. The Fairey aircraft industry was

speechtext: I am sure the hon. member will be congratulated on the job he has done.

I should like some information regarding the contract to supply naval fuel oil for Esquimalt. On June 14 of this year, I was given answers to some questions I had asked regarding the supply of this fuel oil. I was informed that the contract had been let to White Petroleums, who were agents for the Union Oil Company of California. I was informed also that this fuel was derived from foreign crude oil, and that it was being delivered to Esquimalt by the company tankers.
I was rather surprised that we should have been purchasing foreign oil for our naval vessels, in view of the announced policy of the department that, so far as possible, they would obtain the supplies from Canadian sources, and particularly in view of the fact that only recently some $93 million has been spent on the construction of a pipe line from northern Alberta to Vancouver, and that large sums of money have been expended in the construction of refineries. In addition to that, about a million dollars has been spent by Imperial Oil Company to develop a wharf for the oil tankers in Vancouver.
Furthermore, I believe that in the past the fuel oil for the navy had been delivered to Vancouver and it had been conveyed from Vancouver to Esquimalt naval fuel base by the Canadian naval tanker H.M.C.S. Dundurn. So far as I know, that procedure was carried out satisfactorily. I would therefore like to be informed as to the total amount of fuel oil for this year's contract, both bunker and
6470	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production diesel oil, the price which has been paid, and also an explanation as to why it has become necessary to obtain fuel oil from foreign crude, when, it seems to me, at the present time there is an abundance of Alberta oil available on the west coast. In fact we heard only within the last few days of a statement by the president of the Imperial Oil Company, and supported by the executives of other companies out on the west coast, that they expect rather difficult times in being able to find markets for Canadian oil.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I believe I am in an excellent position to answer the question, because when I saw the requisition coming through I thought there must be something wrong with it when they were buying oil in California. I sent it back for a complete explanation. I was not too happy about the explanation I received, so I had an expert in to discuss it.
The cold fact is that west coast consumption-and it must be kept in mind that this is residual oil-the consumption of residual oil is about 17,000 barrels a day, and refinery production in that area is about 7,000 barrels a day. So that about 10,000 barrels of residual oil are being brought into the area every day.
We could have placed the order at a slightly higher cost with Canadian refineries, and taken their residual oil for the navy, which would simply have meant that the ordinary consumer would have been using California oil to that additional extent. The only difference would have been that the crown would have paid the local price, which is somewhat higher than the landed price of California crude, and the difference between the two would have gone to the trade, instead of to the crown.
By buying California residual oil and taking advantage of the lower price and the discount on California crude there was considerable saving in dollars. As I say, the local supply of residual oil is fully utilized. My hon. friend will understand that gasoline is cracked in the Vancouver area. The quantity of residual oil depends wholly upon the demand for gasoline. If that demand is small, then the residual oil produced by the refineries is small. With the "cat-crackers" used there now, we get less and less residual oil as a proportion of the total crude which comes into the refinery.
We were short of the type of fuel oil required, and it was not available at Vancouver. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.

There has been a considerable reduction in the expenditures of this department. The department is a big spending agency and, while it is proper to recognize its accomplishments-and the right hon. gentleman is frequently recognized in glowing terms for his accomplishments

it is also relevant to call attention to the shortcomings of the department in the discharge of its duties. I have no doubt the minister will expect the opposition to call these matters to his attention and to that of hon. members in the committee.
I wish to refer to two items with which the Auditor General was dissatisfied. These are reported at page 20 of the Auditor General's report for 1953. The two items there relate to contracts which, under section 17 of the Defence Production Act, require to be approved by the governor in council. The complaint of the Auditor General is that although the contracts were originally approved by the governor in council subsequent alterations to the advantage of the contractor were made as routine departmental procedure.
The Auditor General has taken the view, and quite properly, that where a contract has initially to follow a certain procedure, any change or alteration should be made only after following the same procedure, that is with the sanction of the governor in council.
In the first instance there was a discount of two per cent which a contractor had agreed to take for payment within thirty days. After the governor in council had dealt with the contract there was an amendment made by which that discount was removed.
In the second instance an allowance was made after a contract had been formally approved.
Then, there is a third item at page 21 about which I should like to ask the minister. In this case it appears that an allowance was made to a firm which had undertaken to make overcoats from cloth supplied by the department. The allowance was necessary because the cloth was found not to be up to specifications. It had shrunk in the course of manufacture, and caused the contractor considerable loss. So far as the contractor was concerned, apparently the department quite properly recognized that it was not the fault of the tailoring firm, and allowed $62,762 as compensation for extra loss by reason of the faulty cloth.
The important point is this: Did the department, which had purchased this cloth and supplied it to the contractor, then follow up

to recover from its supplier the value of the amount it had paid out as damages? It seems to me this could have been recovered properly as damages payable by the supplier of the faulty cloth, which had not been properly shrunk.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite correct in saying that the reason for that payment was that the cloth supplied by the department was defective, in that it shrank. It was not the fault of the contractor. An adjustment was made so that the contractor would escape unharmed. The cloth was drawn from government stores. At that stage it was impossible to trace its origin. The adjustment was debited to the cloth account. My hon. friend will realize we buy our cloth in long runs so as to get the full mill discount. We have perhaps $20 million worth of cloth in store at all times, and that cloth is supplied to contractors for uniforms and for government clothing generally.
_ Apparently there was a mistake in the inspection of the cloth. It was called to everyone's attention, but it was impossible at that stage to trace where the error was made, or even where the cloth came from.

I appreciate that if it was impossible to identify the supplier of the cloth it would be difficult to claim back, as I have suggested. I would like to have the minister's assurance on this point. If the department follows ordinary business practice, such as prevails in private business, then certainly a claim would be made back against the supplier of the cloth.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: And it certainly would have been, if we had been able to identify the supplier at that stage. But it did lead to a tightening up in our inspections. I think all we can say is that we are pretty sure it will not happen again.

I regret very much the minister cannot tell us the number of one of these orders in council, because I have tried to get hold of them and I have been informed that they are now with the treasury board.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, I should have said treasury board minutes. They are all tabled.
I put some questions to the minister this morning with which he has not dealt. Perhaps we could run over them briefly now.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I shall be glad to deal with them, if you like. I was just waiting for the opportunity. The first one I think dealt with the relationship of D.D.P. and Department of National Defence.
Is it the same as it was a year ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Exactly, yes. In other words, the Department of National Defence indicates what is required, writes a specification for the article, determines the place and time of delivery, and from that point the Department of Defence Production takes over and carries out the work at its discretion, subject to inspection and acceptance by the Department of National Defence.
The Department of Defence Production takes no responsibility in regard to quantity or necessity?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No. That of course has first to be approved by the responsible committee of the Department of National Defence. Then it goes to treasury board and is approved there as being reasonable and in accordance with the appropriations of the department. The treasury board authorizes an allotment or financial encumbrance. In other words, at the proper stage we get from the treasury board a financial encumbrance which indicates that certain funds have been encumbered to pay for the material requisitioned. At that stage we take over. We may decide to build a plant to manufacture the article or we may decide to buy it from an existing Canadian plant, or we may decide that the circumstances are such that we should import from outside the country. That is a decision of the Department of Defence Production.
Then, my hon. friend discussed the purchasing policy, as to whether goods should be manufactured in Canada, or, if purchased outside of Canada, whether from the United Kingdom or from the United States; and he indicated it is the free choice of the department. That is hardly the case. Unless there is a substantial saving, the policy is to purchase in Canada, and if the volume is sufficient we will even set up facilities to manufacture in Canada. The strategic situation intervenes there to a point. In other words, if we are building a naval ship, should we manufacture all components in Canada? The


view has been, if we are undertaking to build naval ships in Canada, we should also build the components in Canada so that, in the event of war, we are self-contained in that particular field. But if the situation is that we had been purchasing too much in the United States and too little in the United Kingdom, I would point out that probably more than 50 per cent of our purchases outside of Canada have been in the field of aircraft. In the early stages we have purchased aircraft engines in the United States. It is said that we should have purchased in Britain. Britain herself was buying aircraft and aircraft engines from the United States. I suppose even today Britain's armament includes more F-86's, some manufactured in Canada and some in the United States, and all powered with engines made in North America, than planes of British manufacture with British engines. It would therefore be necessary that aircraft expenditure be largely directed towards the United States. We did undertake to manufacture one training plane, the T-33, and there we were able to buy Rolls-Royce engines in England. There happened to be a line of engines of which they had a small surplus that could be devoted to this purpose; but generally speaking it was not possible, within the last year at least, to buy any substantial aircraft or aircraft parts in the United Kingdom.
Another factor that must be taken into consideration is that the army has adopted United States standards for most of its weapons. We were able to buy our tanks in the United Kingdom. The United States came to the same conclusion, as we did, that the Centurion tank was the best heavy tank being produced anywhere, and we both bought our tanks in the United Kingdom. We also bought an aircraft carrier in the United Kingdom and we are having it modernized in the United Kingdom. Where it has been possible to buy in the United Kingdom we have done so. That has been our policy and as a matter of fact we never lose an opportunity to buy in the United Kingdom rather than in the United States. The nature of our armament is such that we have been forced to buy very heavily in the United States.
I might point out that the United States has also bought armament from Canada. The accounts are not in balance, but they are not far out. In the year 1953 the United States bought more in Canada than we bought in the United States. That is a factor we must keep in mind in connection with purchases in the United States. Capital assistance is provided only when a certain product is needed and no other avenue is open except by paying capital assistance

either to equip the plant with specialized machinery or to build an addition to the existing plant.
May I interrupt the minister there? Did I understand him to say that last year the United States government spent more on defence procurement in Canada than Canada spent in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is my recollection, although I can check.

I think the minister is wrong. If he will look at the table in his report at page 50, appendix F, it will be seen that the United States government's expenditures on defence procurement in Canada during 1953 amounted to $127 million, whereas table 8, page 49, shows that the Canadian government expenditures on defence procurement in the United States for 1953 amounted to $129,724,000. In addition to that we find that, according to page 47, Canadian defence orders placed in the United States in 1953 amounted to $61 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I had in mind the procurement figures, which are a little different.
Even there we bought a little more from them than they from us during 1953.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: In the fiscal year 1953-54 we paid them $107 million and they paid us $126 million. The orders placed go the other way. I am talking about the actual payments, not the deliveries.
Can the minister say what expenditures the Department of Defence Production made in purchases for civil defence, which would presumably be for the Department of National Health and Welfare?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We have bought articles on requisition for the civil defence organization. We bought pumpers and blankets. They are not obliged to buy through the department but they frequently do so. I do not know what they buy outside the department.

I take it the same situation does not obtain as between the Department of Defence Production and the Department of National Health and Welfare, on the one hand, as exists between the Department of Defence Production and the Department of National Defence, on the other. In other words, the Department of National Health and Welfare makes only a limited use of the purchasing facilities of the Department of Defence Production in matters pertaining to civil defence?
Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The minister has told me that we buy everything he buys, so I would say that the situation is exactly the same as exists with respect to the Department of National Defence.

On page 21 of the report we have the statement:
The United States, however, remained the largest single source of supply for machine tools.
This matter of machine tools is one of some importance and I wonder if the minister can hold out some hope that we are not going to continue to be so dependent on the United States for that important commodity.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That situation arose because of availability. At the beginning of the Korean war there was a great rush to buy machine tools. We bought all we could in England, the United States, and a few from the continent because work was being held up owing to the lack of machine tools. Of course, that is not the situation today. I doubt if the department has bought many machine tools in the United States for some months. In the early days of Korea it was a question of availability, and the situation was exactly the same at the beginning of the second world war.
Could the minister tell us what proportion of the expenditure made through his department last year was made on purchases without calling tenders?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: These figures go back to the beginning. Of all orders placed on behalf of the Department of National Defence, 4-4 per cent were negotiated contracts. Of orders placed in Canada on behalf of the Department of National Defence, excluding foreign contracts, negotiated contracts amounted to 2-3 per cent. Of orders over $10,000 placed in Canada, negotiated orders amounted to 4-4 per cent. Very little is left in the way of negotiated cost-plus orders today for we are able to establish the price of everything either on a fixed price basis or an incentive basis.

Would the minister say more about that? There is quite a lot of concern in regard to the matter of purchasing without tenders and also in relation to cost-plus contracts. I think we would like to hear a fuller explanation in regard to the matter of purchases without tender under present conditions, because it is quite apparent that the market conditions under which the department is now purchasing are very different from those under which the department was purchasing a year or two ago. We would be glad to hear about the extent to which the department has been able to abandon the
6474	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production cost-plus contract in favour of what the minister has called the "incentive contract".

If we get a requisition for, say, CF-lOO's there is only one place we can buy them and that is from the manufacturer. You could hardly call for tenders on CF-lOO's, and in that case the best we can do is to negotiate a basis for production. It may not be a cost-plus contract but it certainly is a negotiated contract. In addition, if we want to buy General Motors transmissions, and we do buy a considerable quantity because they are standard in our larger motor transports, then we have to go to General Motors to buy them. In other words, we cannot call for competitive tenders when there is only one source of supply. It might easily be a firm price, but in most cases it is a negotiated price and must necessarily be so. There are certain things in which we have a choice and for which we call for tenders.

May we take it that in the case of anything in the nature of a product that is to some extent a standardized and not a custom product the department is firmly adhering to the policy of purchasing by tender?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Invariably.
Will the minister then make some further comment about the extent to which the department is abandoning the cost-plus contract in favour of the incentive contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I think it has been months since we have placed a cost-plus contract on construction. We had a case where we were doing secret radar work and using plans furnished by the United States. We were not allowed to distribute these plans generally and therefore we had no option but to place a cost-plus contract. That, however, was an unusual case and I know of no similar case since that occasion. At certain remote spots where it would obviously be too expensive to send in two contractors to estimate a job we sometimes place a cost-plus contract. I think Churchill is a case in point, though later contracts there have not been issued on a cost-plus basis. I am told that over the last year or so we have been getting excellent competition on almost every type of construction regardless of where located.
What is the nature of this incentive contract to which the minister referred?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
This type of contract is normally used in manufacturing. The contractor and the government agree that a


certain price is a reasonable price at a certain stage of production. If by extra skill the contractor is then able to produce for less than that price, he gets a bonus on his fee. If on the other hand his production costs more than the target price, he gets a smaller fee than the contract would otherwise call for.
You are not applying that procedure under any construction contracts? It is only on manufacturing contracts that you apply that incentive?
