Mr. Chairman, I am interested in this case because of a particular point that is raised by it. It is a matter I have taken the trouble to do some reading about, and I think it should be of interest to members of the house who are members of the medical profession and also to those who are members of the legal profession. My reading on the subject which is raised by this case led me in particular to examine a very excellent paper entitled "Medical Privilege" which was given by Mr. Justice Samuel Freedman of the court of queen's bench, Winnipeg, Manitoba, at a recent meeting of the Manitoba medico-legal society at Winnipeg. Mr. Justice Freedman was dealing in this article with the question as to whether or not there should be extended to medical practitioners throughout Canada the protection in courts which is enjoyed by members of the legal profession. The reason I read the article and the reason I want to make some references to it is because that question arose in connection with this case.
I do not wish to put any names on Hansard so I will use letters where I wish to delete names. But with that qualification I should like to read an extract from page 12 of the evidence in the case now before us under Bill No. 451. One of the examiners who was asking questions before the committee in the other place said:
Q. Mrs. X, Dr. Y cannot be required to reveal any information he may have received by examining or treating you in his professional capacity, but you have the right if you wish to permit him to do so-to consent that he do so and give him that authority. You do not have to give him that authority if you do not want to.
[The Deputy Chairman.]

By the Chairman: You understand that, that you may give him permission to tell us what was the result of his findings?
A. Yes.
Q. You are willing to do that?
A. Yes, I am.
I will not bother to read the next part of the proceedings which is the evidence given by the physician whom I have characterized as Dr. Y and which became rather important evidence in connection with this application for divorce. In fact, after this doctor had given his evidence the chairman of the committee, Senator Roebuck, said:
That is very good evidence. Thank you, very much.
There is no question about it that the evidence was the kind of evidence that was useful in a case such as this. I wish to make it clear that the woman in question did give her consent to this medical man giving evidence before the Senate committee which he had gained in his professional capacity as an attending physician. The point I raise is to me a very interesting one. Was it appropriate for it to be suggested in a hearing in a committee of the parliament of Canada, on the soil of the province of Ontario, if you will, that a doctor could not be required to give evidence obtained in his professional capacity? It is in that connection that I find this lecture by my friend, Mr. Justice Samuel Freedman, very interesting. He tells us that the basis of the law regarding medical privilege so far as the United Kingdom is concerned and so far as Canada is concerned, except for the province of Quebec, goes away back to 1776. He says:
It is the year 1776. The scene is Westminster Hall, and the occasion is the trial before the Right Hon. the House of Peers of Elizabeth, Duchess of Kingston, for bigamy. The noble lady is charged with having gone through a form of marriage with the Duke of Kingston while her first husband, Augustus John Hervey, later Earl of Bristol, was still-

On a point of order, I should like to point out to the hon. member that, while this doubtless may be a most fascinating legal point for him to discuss, it has no relevancy whatsoever to the decision in the case before us. I would point out, purely on the grounds of relevancy, that what the hon. member is discussing has nothing to do with the decision of this house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am thoroughly in agreement with the ruling you have made from time to time, even if that ruling sometimes impinges upon what I would like to say myself, that in discussing these bills we should discuss the particular case that is before us at any one time. I have

accepted your stricture that we must not wander off into a discussion as to what happened with respect to other bills. But I submit that when we have before us a bill, the major portion of the evidence of which is based on what was stated by a doctor, I have the right to raise the question as to the propriety of it being said in the committee of the other house that there was such a thing as medical privilege on which that doctor and that patient could rely. My purpose in referring to the paper given by Mr. Justice Freedman is to prove my point that medical privilege does not obtain in the courts of Canada outside of the province of Quebec. If it is uninteresting or distasteful for me to read at length from Mr. Justice Freedman's article, I am prepared to curtail my quotations from this article, but I think there is no question but that I should be permitted to quote sufficiently from this article to prove my point that medical privilege in the courts of this country, with the exception of those in the province of Quebec, does not apply. It is that that I want to establish from Mr. Justice Freedman's article. If Your Honour wishes to make a ruling on that point, I will sit down until the ruling is made.

speechtext: May I ask a question, Mr. Chairman? If my hon. friend satisfies himself that in fact there is no such privilege, do I take it that he then feels that the evidence was not sufficient and he is going to oppose this particular bill?

By way of compromise, I shall certainly reduce what I had intended to do by way of quoting from the article by Mr. Justice Freedman. He gives a very interesting history of this question, but ends up by saying:
Were this paper concerned merely with a declaration of the law on whether a doctor is entitled to professional privilege it could end at this point. Our law is clear. He has no such right.
Later in the article or in the footnotes, Mr. Justice Freedman makes it clear that in Quebec there is such a privilege. Indeed, in the Quebec civil code it is provided that a witness cannot be compelled to declare what has been revealed to him confidentially in his professional character as a religious or legal adviser, or as an officer of state where public policy is concerned. This provision covers religious and legal people, but then in the Quebec medical act, section 60, subsection 2, there is the following provision:
No physician may be compelled to declare what has been revealed to him in his professional character.
Mr. Justice Freedman points out that that privilege applies in Quebec, and that is the only place in Canada where it applies. That being the case, I submit it does not apply in Ontario, and in this instance the hearing was held within the territorial limits of the province of Ontario. The doctor in question was an Ontario doctor residing in Kingston. The patient whom he had examined had been examined at Kingston, and yet it was suggested to him that he had a privilege which does not obtain.
Now, one of the problems involved in all of this and the difficulty in dealing with cases like this, where at least one of the parties is a resident in a province where they do not want divorce courts, is that in this case the law of that province was imported into the proceedings held here at Ottawa. I feel it was quite wrong for the senators to take that position. Perhaps there is a case for changing the law with regard to medical

privilege. Mr. Justice Freedman does not come to that conclusion. He feels the law should not be changed.
As I say, I rose not to discuss the details of the case itself, except with respect to this one point. Whether or not the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration accepts my judgment, I submit with due respect for his judgment that Their Honours were wrong when they imported into a hearing on Ontario soil a provision that applies in Quebec but does not apply anywhere else in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I hope there is no feeling that I would not accept my hon. friend's judgment on occasion, but I have really not the time to come to a conclusion about the law of medical privilege. I have looked at it off and on for something approaching 30 years, but I do not feel I could discuss it learnedly in 40 minutes like my hon. friend. For that reason,
I do not know how he could come to the conclusion he has stated in that regard in such a short time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

I believe it is a question of whether or not the law of the province of Quebec can be pleaded in Ontario. Perhaps the hon. member is not aware of the fact that the law of a person's domicile will follow him into any other province in Canada. If the province of Quebec is this man's domicile, he can plead that law in the province of Ontario as it affects the person.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am glad the hon. member for Cartier has raised that point. I thought I had answered it. The doctor and the patient are both residents of the province of Ontario, and the hearing took place in Ontario. The point the hon. member has made would have been valid had it been a Quebec doctor or evidence on behalf of a Quebec patient, but it was an Ontario doctor who had examined an Ontario patient in the province of Ontario.

I am convinced, Mr. Chairman, this discussion is entirely out of order. After all, the Senate divorce committee is not bound by the rules of evidence of any province of Canada. It is bound by the rules under which it operates. A discussion here of whether or not they have the right to do this or that has no relevancy whatever. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre


must realize that the committee is not bound by those rules, and the discussion is entirely out of order.

Surely it is proper for this committee to look into the evidence, and if there is something wrong with the evidence, something with which they disagree, it would be proper to draw the attention of this house to that and, perhaps as in the other case, have it referred back to the private bills committee.
I would think that would be a most improper thing. If the hon. member wishes to reform the rules of the Senate committee, I would suggest he move over there and do what he can.

This case is typical of the problems that come to us when we read the evidence. As mentioned by my colleague, the hon. member for Yorkton, the petitioner is a soldier on active service in Korea. Apparently there were some domestic troubles shortly after the couple were married, but I feel it is unfortunate that the petitioner was not given a chance to come back from Korea to appear in person and to state whether or not he was prepared to try again.
The evidence that appears in connection with Bill No. 451 would indicate that the petitioner's wife has not been loyal to him during his absence. In view of the fact he is the one seeking the divorce, I feel he might have been called. I noticed that the question of collusion is raised in connection with this case. I am sure that the hon. member for Victoria, on reading this evidence along with the evidence in many more cases, will certainly consider there is every indication there is collusion in connection with these cases.
Apparently the soldier in Korea has information concerning the misconduct of his wife, and also has information concerning the man who has come into the home to break up the home. As a matter of fact, apparently the man who has come into the picture was here in Ottawa. When the solicitor for the petitioner mentioned that the man was here in attendance but did not think it necessary to call him, the chairman said, "I do not think so; I think we will recommend the case." The case was recommended.
I would say that it was unfortunate the soldier was not given a chance to come home from Korea. If there was a big hurry to get this through, if an injustice had been done to him during the time he was away, I think the least that could have been done was to have him brought back and given a chance to appear in person. As I said, it is difficult to assess these cases when members of the house do not have an opportunity to hear the people

involved. Even after one does hear the people involved, as was the case with one other petition, it would appear that a committee of this house is not able to deal with the matter properly. I hope that we will be relieved of the responsibility of deciding whether or not the recommendation made by the other house should be accepted in cases of this sort.

Mr. Chairman, first of all
may I echo the sentiments of the Secretary of State when he says that he hopes we will not much longer have to go through this very nasty procedure which, I am sure, is distasteful to all of us. So far as I am concerned, I would say, "How long, O Lord, how long?" But so long as I am a member of the miscellaneous private bills committee and a member of the House of Commons I intend to see that at least some of these cases shall have thorough consideration. That is as I see my duty in the matter.
I am a member of the miscellaneous private bills committee, and I was in the room when these ten bills, of which this is one, were considered. I have noticed that my hon. friend, the hon. member for Parkdale, the chairman of that committee, and a gentleman for whom I have the greatest respect, has

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Private Bills-Divorce interjected remarks on two or three occasions. I had not intended to say anything of what I shall now say but under the circumstances perhaps I had better do so, because it is not only the committee in the other place that can make mistakes.
There is always of course the question as to whether these bills should be considered en bloc or considered one at a time. And by the way, before I forget what I wish to say, let me give notice here and now to the members of the miscellaneous private bills committee, and to the various counsel who appear in divorce cases, that so long as I am on that committee and there is before it a contested divorce, whether others take this procedure or not I will do my part to see that such a case is thoroughly reviewed by that committee.
As usual, in the committee I made my little protest, in which I said that I was in favour of considering these bills one by one. I appealed to the chairman and he replied, "Mr. Knight must know that that is not in my hands, and it is not in the hands of the committee." I am not criticizing the chairman, because I suppose he is only human. There was nothing I could do about it. So one of the members of the committee who supports the government offered a motion that the bills be considered en bloc. Hon. members will know of course what the result was. Hon. members in this group who were protesting were defeated by a vote. I may say I asked for a recorded vote on that particular occasion. He who runs may read, because the vote is recorded, and the names of those who asked that the bills be considered en bloc are on record with the clerk of one of the committees of the house.
I do not want to go into that phase of the matter at too great length. We continued to consider the contested case, for which counsel appeared and witnesses were called on both sides. Apparently everyone was in a hurry, and the ten bills were passed- 1,2,3,4,5,6-like that. No, I should not say, "1,2,3,4,5,6"-I should say simply 1 to 10. And so we were ready for the next case, about which I shall have something to say when it comes up on the next occasion, which I presume will be Friday of this week, if the house is still sitting.
However, the result of the whole thing was that the committee had to be called back next morning and the procedure had to be repeated painfully again because, as every hon. member knows-and I certainly did know-a committee, whether it be a private bills committee, or something else, is simply an extension of the committee of the whole house. And, as is stated in

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Beauchesne, what rules the House of Commons rules the conduct of that committee. The procedure is laid down, and is not in the hands of the committee.
That was the story of those ten bills and we did pass them at the next sitting of the committee. The result is that they are now back in the House of Commons. I should like now for a moment to talk about the particular bill before us.
The hon. member for Wellington South and I had some argument in committee about collusion, and I referred him to his Latin dictionary. This is a case where I certainly suspect collusion. It is a peculiar case. Like my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, I am not going to mention names, but this case refers to an Englishman who came out to this country and settled in the city of Montreal. He married an English lady and after a space of time the lady went back to Great Britain and is now living there. She did not appear at all before the Senate committee.
My learned friends will know the term-I do not-but the fact is that counsel backed up her petition with some kind of sworn statement over there. That was the way the petition was presented to the Senate committee. And then the most amazing thing happened. This respondent, this man who was accused of adultery-and one would almost think he was proud of the fact- became the principal witness for the petitioner. My hon. friend and I had a disagreement. He said it did not involve collusion. Well, if it is not collusion, then I do not know the meaning of the word.
Let me read from the evidence-and my hon. friend will not expect me, I know, to mention names, because I have no taste for this sort of thing. I do not like to see these names dragged out before the public and recorded in Hansard. But here is part of the evidence. This question was asked:
Has there been any collusion or agreement between you and your wife in order to obtain this divorce?
The respondent said: "No." Then, Mr. Lapin, who I presume was the counsel, warned the witness. He said:
The witness does not have to answer questions as to adultery.
If the respondent had not answered questions as to the adultery and implicated himself in doing so, then the divorce would not have been granted. Then we come down to the further question. In this instance again Mr. Lapin asked:
In your wife's petition your wife complains that between the 25th of March and some time in April you committed adultery with

.Is that true?

I can almost see him clapping his chest and saying: Yes, that is me; I am the man. Well, that is it. That was the evidence on which the divorce was granted.
He was bragging.

He was bragging, but I do not know what about. It is not something that a man should brag about. The chairman of the committee in the other place seemed to be rather surprised and said: If you have another witness you may call him.
Apparently he was surprised that any other witness was needed. Then this respondent who was so willing to confess before the committee that he was an adulterer said that he had another fellow there, a personal friend. He produced the friend who said, yes, my friend has told me many times, and so on. He said a few things that are flavourable but not favourable, and on that basis this divorce was simply granted. I suggest that if there was not collusion, then I for one do not know what collusion is. My hon. friend says he knows the meaning of the word but I do not, if this is not a case of collusion.

Mr. Chairman, this is one of 462 bills which have been presented to the Senate committee at this session. It is true that 63 of these bills were not proceeded with, the reason being that they were presented too late and I suppose in the normal course of events they will come before us next year. However, of this total 382 were recommended by the Senate, and three were rejected by the Senate. It will therefore be seen that in most of these cases the evidence must have been pretty good or at least satisfying

to the Senate committee. Fourteen were withdrawn, one of which turned out to be the rather notorious case which I shall not mention here.
In regard to this particular bill I think it would be a good thing if we looked into its history as it passed through its various stages. In the first place, this bill was presented to the Senate committee which passed it and a divorce was recommended. It then came into this house for first reading and as is usual in the case of most bills it did not receive very detailed consideration on that first reading. It then came up for second reading and was passed, again without consideration. It then came into committee and it was only by sheerest accident that one of my colleagues noticed it was a contested case and by the bulk of the evidence it appeared as though there had been considerable argument. He took the case up and read it through. In committee of the whole he spoke on the bill and then the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre at the end of that day's debate moved that the bill be not now read a third time but that it be sent back to the miscellaneous private bills committee for further consideration.
The vote on that motion in this house is now past history. The house voted by 66 to 63, presumably upon the reading of the evidence or upon the validity of the arguments advanced by my colleague, to send it back, and the bill which had already passed the infallible committee in the other place, and passed its first and second readings in this house was recommended to be sent back to the miscellaneous private bills committee for further consideration.
I want to point out that we who are members of that committee are sometimes placed in an unfortunate position. There was one famous case which was before the committee last year and it was discovered that a minor technical mistake had been made. The committee was called back the next morning so that the chairman could put in the words: "Shall I report the bill?" The next day there were three times as many members attending that committee and I think it is fair to say that most of them came from the government side of the house. The case was re-opened and the decision reversed.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, how does the hon. gentleman relate that to the bill now before the committee?

I am just coming to the bill. I know the Secretary of State is wondering why we should have to put up with this kind of stuff and I agree with him, but I am now going to relate this to the bill now before us.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If I may clear up the first point with respect to these plants being in competition with privately-owned industries, that is not the case. If privately-owned industries were able to do the job we would not have built the plants. These plants are built for special purposes. It sounds quite logical to my hon. friend to say that we should pay whatever the municipality assesses, but there are several factors that interfere with that. One is that we often furnish services that other plants would expect to receive from the municipality. That is one factor. Another factor is that under the British North America Act the crown is not liable for taxes. Therefore instead of paying taxes we make a grant in lieu of taxes, but the grant is generally comparable to the taxes that a privately-owned plant would pay under exactly the same circumstances. Often it is a bit more than the privately-owned plant is paying. Usually privately-owned plants have tax deals going back many years which protect them today. Civil defence-
288. To provide for the civil defence program, $6,498,253.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Does the minister wish to say anything on this important subject at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Not at this time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that this subject is of great importance to the life of this country and even though the session may be far advanced and we are all hoping to return to our homes in the near future, I do believe that some words should be said on this matter. I should like to offer a few observations. During the past day, and previous to that during the month of May, we were discussing the estimates of the Department of National Defence. We have passed in the estimates for that department the sum of approximately $2 billion, but I must call attention to the fact that the armed forces would be quite useless, no matter how strong they might be, if the civilian base of this country were knocked out and if the will of the civilian population were destroyed.
So far as the defence of this continent is concerned, the responsibility of the armed forces, of course, would be to keep the attacking enemy as far away as possible from our Canadian cities. It would also be the responsibility of the armed forces, I should think, to provide the civil defence organization and the peoples of the land with as early warning as possible. Having discharged those duties, it would seem to me that the responsibility for limiting the damage which might be caused, taking care of the casualties and mitigating the general suffering which would be inherent with that attack, would be the responsibility of the civil organization. I do not believe we can be so optimistic as to think we can stop every bomber from getting through. Some will get through to their target, but we trust that the numbers will be extremely few.
If any bombers do get through, many of the essential services will be destroyed. It will be the responsibility, therefore, of the civil organization to restore those essential services and ensure that there is as little disruption as possible to the general life of the country. I think, in broad general terms, that might be considered as an indication of the sort of tasks, the sort of objectives, of any civil defence organization which exists.
Supply-Health and Welfare
Some four or five years ago in this house I suggested that the responsibility for civil defence be removed from the Department of National Defence to some other department. Shortly after I had made that suggestion- no doubt other people had made it before- the Prime Minister removed the responsibility for civil defence from national defence to national health and welfare, thereby, rightly in my opinion, emphasizing the essentially civilian nature of civil defence. After all, civil defence really boils down to a scheme, in the main voluntary, in which one neighbour prepares himself to help another neighbour in the event of the dire results of a war and an attack upon this country.
I believe that the neighbourly nature of civil defence should be emphasized. I, for one, do not regard civil defence as a sort of fourth arm of the fighting services. Some people do. Since that day when civil defence was placed under the Minister of National Health and Welfare there have been considerable strides made in the development of our civil defence organization. Only those who fail to appreciate the difficulties that confront any department which tries to build up an organization which is essentially voluntary, the objects of which are rather nebulous, would dare say that the scheme for civil defence to date has been a failure. I do not believe that, and I should like to go on record as paying tribute to all those people who have taken part in building up the organization, from the minister and his staff here in Ottawa to the permanently employed officials in the various provinces and municipalities and the thousands of voluntary workers who have come forward and given of their time to try and create this great scheme for civil defence.
If the development and progress can be recorded, at the same time I do not think we can sit back and say that the progress is entirely satisfactory and that we do not feel that further endeavours should be made. The amount of progress which can be achieved will, to a certain extent, depend upon the funds which are voted by this parliament. I notice that when the present minister took over this department he had to get through as best he could with what I described as a very meagre amount, some $2 million. I notice that in more recent times the amount has advanced to somewhere in the neighbourhood of $6-5 million. I do not think that amount of money has been spent during the last year. There may be reasons why the sums voted by parliament for civil defence have not been spent. At the same time I feel it is highly desirable that the department should take full

Supply

Health and Welfare advantage of the funds which are made available by this parliament for the purposes for which they are allocated.
The general system, so far as I know, for the allocation of funds is that the federal government contributes dollar for dollar with each province. Each province has to be prepared and willing to enter into that dominion-provincial scheme. I regret to say that all the provinces have not agreed to go into that scheme and therefore we find that progress throughout the country is varied. In some provinces where they are keenly alive to the necessity of civil defence, and where the provincial contributions have been generous and have been matched by the dominion grants, there can be seen definite progress.
But as there are still some provinces I believe which have not entered into the scheme, such information as I have would indicate that the progress has not been as satisfactory in those provinces. In spite of the lack of any provincial grant, some municipalities in those provinces have made very considerable grants out of their civil funds, and I think a great deal of credit is due to those cities and urban centres where they have made contributions out of their very limited resources which, unfortunately, cannot be matched by the federal grants because those federal grants are allocated only for the help of the provinces. However some assistance can be given in the way of equipment.
Until there is a uniform system throughout the country, and a recognition on the part of all levels of government as to their own responsibility, and until those responsibilities are clearly defined, we shall never have a uniform system of civil defence across the whole of our land. It seems to me we are now threatened with what amounts to a new look, so far as civil defence is concerned; because the original civil defence plan was designed, first of all, to take care of the casualties and the damage caused by the ordinary high explosive bombs. From there they moved forward to the Hiroshima type of attack, by the A-bomb. Now we have reached the position where there is a far more deadly bomb, sometimes referred to as the H-bomb, and which is known to be in the possession of many powers.
Therefore it would be foolish for civil defence merely to base its plans for organization on the assumption that we might be attacked only with high explosive or even with A-bombs. The devastating effect of an H-bomb is, shall we say-and I do not think I am exaggerating-ten times as great as might have been experienced from an A-bomb of the type used at the end of the war.


Instead of only partially destroying a limited area in a city we must fact the fact that it is possible now for whole cities to be destroyed.
And so I say we have to take a new look at our civil defence. And if we are going to do that, then it seems to me now is the time when we have to invest real authority in the hands of the minister responsible for the department, and when we have to give him a constitutional position backed by an act of parliament. I think the time has now come for the government to give serious consideration to the introduction of a civil defence act. This is not a new or original idea. There are civil defence acts in existence in the United Kingdom, in the United States and in several of our provinces. But in this country where we have a federation, and where a great deal of autonomy is vested in the various provincial governments, I feel that in a matter which transcends boundaries between provinces and where co-ordination is required from the Atlantic to the Pacific now is the time for the government to introduce a civil defence act.
I make that suggestion to the minister because I know that all matters dealing with civil defence are the concern of many different departments. Obviously one realizes at once the interdependence of civil defence with the Department of National Defence. But then one need only stop for a moment to realize that civil defence is very closely related to other departments. Obviously, if there is going to be a destruction of public services, then the Department of Public Works would be very closely related with the work of civil defence. It would be closely related, not only after a bomb had fallen but in the preparatory stages before an attack.
For instance one of the major threats in civil defence matters today is the necessity of evacuating many of the larger cities. Exercises were carried out in a northwestern state recently in which large cities were evacuated, and most important lessons were drawn from that plan for mass evacuation. In a country where so many of our cities are located on rivers, and where our highways are limited, it can easily be seen that in the preparation for the evacuation of any of our large cities it might be necessary to have an extensive public works program. Perhaps one might have to provide additional bridges or tunnels, or to make new highways leading out of cities. All those things are very closely related to civil defence planning. Transport enters into the question. Of course the railways have to be kept running and the mails must be delivered. There must be protection against the possibility of sabotage.

The Department of Justice enters into the picture because there would be all kinds of legal matters. And so, without enlarging on the point, I feel some sort of committee of ministers may have to be set up; and certainly the various departments will have to have persons allocated as secretaries for civil defence matters in those particular departments.
I think the time has now come when not only should we have an act governing civil defence regulations, but that there should be an official at the level of a deputy minister who would be in charge of civil defence, who would be able to confer with senior officials in other departments, and who would have to have seniority sufficient to permit him to attend meetings of chiefs of staff.
Then you say: What subjects would a civil defence act be expected to cover? Well, I can only outline these. My ideas are drawn from existing civil defence acts. For instance, the responsibility of the civil defence minister would be defined in relation to any civil defence services which exist. There are a limited number of regularly employed civil defence personnel. At the present time they are in the main restricted to instructors in the various provinces. I am not certain that an expansion is not required in that respect.
In other countries there is the idea of flying columns or very mobile columns of civil defence workers who are always ready and available. One can see in the thickly-settled portions of our country in eastern Canada the value which would accrue from having a number of flying columns located outside of the principal cities so that they could move in, in case of a disaster. Those flying columns, at least some of them, should be permanently enrolled, and those that are permanently enrolled during the time when there is no threat could be used, it seems to me, as administrators and instructors.
Then of course the majority of the corps of civil defence workers would be those who are not permanently employed in civil defence work, and there are that great mass of men and women who are voluntarily giving their services at this time. But surely responsibility rests on the shoulders of the minister in so far as those voluntary workers are concerned, and obviously the definition of those responsibilities would be laid out in any act.
Furthermore, there is the whole question of the storage of essential equipment. If one is going to work on the assumption that evacuation may be necessary in certain areas, provision has to be made for the caring of the people who have been moved out of some 83276-410i
Supply-Health and Welfare city, and who will at least for the time being" have to sojourn in the rural districts surrounding that city that may be the target. Whether the bombs have fallen in that city or not, anyway, for the time being the care of those people will have to be looked after.
There are bound to be questions regarding the acquisition of land for the building of shelters, report centres and that sort of thing. There will be much that will be required along these lines. Therefore, I feel there are many responsibilities which have to be clearly defined, and can only be clearly defined and can only be given a legal status if they are incorporated in an act of parliament.
Then comes the question of the financial responsibility between the various provinces. We cannot go on any longer in this haphazard way of saying that if a province wishes to make a contribution for civil defence, then the federal government will match its contribution. We have got past the day when it is purely a local responsibility.
Earlier I indicated that there may be some major construction works which would be required if we are working on the thought of possible evacuation of certain areas, or even if we are providing some sort of shelters for essential plants, industrial work, or organizational headquarters. It seems to me that the construction of those major projects should and must be undertaken by the federal government. I do not think that you can place the responsibility of developing a major constructional project upon some local organization. I suggest that it will be essential that we have drawn up in this act a very clear definition as to responsibility as it exists between the various levels of government. I do feel that if the time has not come when the federal government is prepared to take over the full responsibility for civil defence, certainly the time has arrived when the federal government must take over responsibility for the major constructional projects which are required under what I have referred to as the "new look" which must be given to civil defence.
If there is a sudden emergency we may expect that the army is in training or in the process of mobilization in Canada and will be able to take over some of the duties of civil defence in the early stages of any war; but if the army is called upon to do that you are delaying the important tasks which confront the army because in those early days of mobilization any distraction from the process of organizing units and training men only delays and may very easily be disastrous with respect to the army's entry into the war. Therefore I feel that one has to have

Supply-Health and Welfare the civil defence organization in existence in peacetime. You do not want the full organization, but there must be a nucleus around which you can build up very rapidly the required services.
I have mentioned the question of the importance of having mobile columns outside of the cities. I go one step further. I am not satisfied that the mobile columns should be more and more equipped with motor vehicles, but I think you have to have them airborne and possibly using helicopters so that they can enter into a devastated area. They are the key people who would be able to take charge at once, who will be able to restore the broken services and will be able to supervise the voluntary workers who will be partially trained.
I feel there is a danger in relying too much upon the armed forces to provide that essential work, and in fact I have from the very beginning stressed what I consider to be the civilian nature of civil defence. I see great need for skilled traffic control personnel provided by men who have had experience in organizing great parades or supervising spectators going to some large sporting event.
I hope the minister, before these estimates are put through, will be able to outline what progress has been made. I should feel happy if he would say that he is prepared to introduce at the next session of parliament a civil defence act, because I do not believe we are going to make any progress until we get an act of that nature. In addition, before the estimates are concluded I hope the minister will be able to tell us something about the financial responsibilities as between the different layers of government. I do not think this haphazard take it or leave it attitude is satisfactory, and it does not assure the sort of co-ordinated scheme covering Canada that we need at the present time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take advantage of this occasion to say a few words on this important matter of civil defence. It is a subject which should be of utmost concern to every citizen because it comes so close to the very life of every person in Canada. Great progress has been made by the department of national welfare in the past few years and I am glad the Minister of National Health and Welfare is in the house at this time because he has shown an intensive interest in the organization of this branch of his department. The best evidence of his determination to do something about civil defence is the fact that no less than 650 Canadian community civil defence organizations are now in existence.


In more than 200 communities, of which St. Catharines and Lincoln county is an outstanding example, these services are organized and personnel are being trained. The remainder are now in various stages of organization, training, and development. To man these organizations throughout the country more than 163,000 people have been enrolled for various important duties. It is hoped that this total, which includes civil government employees and citizen volunteers, will be substantially increased over the next 12 months.
I have made mention of the extent of local organization across the country because it is local effort and individual initiative that is of importance in the problem of civil defence. I agree with the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich when he says that civil defence should not be the fourth arm of the army. I think civil defence is a task which should be assumed by the citizens in our country in a neighbourly fashion so that neighbours are working together for their self-preservation. Most localities have tackled the problem in a realistic manner, but in some municipalities the effort has fallen far short of what is required if we are to give adequate protection to our citizens.
We have a great need for civil defence in Canada. While Canada, with other freedom-loving nations, is making every effort to secure world peace by mediation and diplomatic negotiation at the United Nations, and by building up a bulwark against aggression through the instrument of NATO, we must recognize that the threat of war is ever present. It is well for us to make reasonable preparation for the protection of our civilian population and of essential public services now existing within our communities.
At one time in our history, wars were fought on distant battlefields, far distant from the civilian community. But today, with the evolution of guided missiles and atomic warfare, war has been brought to our very doorsteps. We cannot enjoy a sense of security even in our own homes. Should a major conflagration take place in this country then civil defence will be our first requirement. It has been said, and said quite rightly, that civil defence has added a third dimension to citizenship, namely, the obligation to protect ourselves and our homes from direct enemy attack.
The targets for any possible future enemy attack would be our heavy industrial installations; our hydroelectric developments; and our transportation systems on the land, in the air and on the water. Within the past week I read, as no doubt did other hon. members, a pamphlet known as The

Bulletin published by the Canadian Industrial Preparedness Association and in the course of an article on management in civil defence it is asserted that it is the individual responsibility of management to take care of civil defence in their own line of business. The article continues:
To assist plant management, the federal civil defence co-ordinator has in process of publication a revised "Civil Defence Manual No. 6" which deals with industrial plant protection. It should soon be available in quantity, either directly or through provincial co-ordinators. This manual in itself is able to give only an outline, but it does lay down the principles involved and suggests steps to be taken.
I am sure that industrialists throughout our country will avail themselves of the opportunity to develop a civil defence organization within their own plants. It is probable that these key locations I have mentioned would be the centres of strategic importance most likely to be attacked.
Steps have been taken by the federal government to provide a system of advance warning so that provincial and local organizations can be alerted to the danger of enemy air attack. The armed forces have established a radar system across the northern part of this country to detect and identify unknown aircraft which might come within our borders. But once the warning has been given the local civil defence organization comes into operation.
The aims of civil defence are to reduce loss of life; to avoid confusion among the local citizens; to provide medical and nursing assistance; to restore public utilities that might be blown up; to minimize property damage, and to ensure the continuation of essential industries. Those are the problems that concern our civil defence organizations if we should be attacked.
I have emphasized already what I believe are the essential steps to be followed in the successful establishment of civil defence groups. In order to establish a strong local committee it is necessary to supply strong, aggressive, and courageous leadership. We, in the county of Lincoln, have been fortunate in finding an individual with such qualities in the person of Brigadier General R. Gordon Whitelaw. Brigadier Whitelaw distinguished himself by his outstanding service in two world wars.
He has thrown himself into the work of civil defence organization in an enthusiastic and vigorous manner. His hours are long; his effort is tremendous and he serves without remuneration of any kind. I wish to express publicly my thanks to Brigadier General Gordon Whitelaw for his unselfish
Supply-Health and Welfare devotion to duty in this field of endeavour. Brigadier Whitelaw has gathered about him a corps of outstanding people with a spirit of community interest, including merchants, industrialists, factory employees, professional people, and agriculturists who are giving of their time and effort providing a strong organization in our community.
Brigadier Whitelaw tells me he feels that a reasonable start can be made only by educating the general public to the dangers that are around us and the need for the protection of our citizens. Three series of articles were published by the local group in the St. Catharines Standard, the local press. Two panel discussions have been broadcast over radio station CKTB and over 8,000 pamphlets on personal survival have been distributed in the local area. A civil defence week was observed last October when two special programs were staged in all local theatres. The John Labatt civil defence disaster convoy was brought in for demonstration in Thorold, Merritton and St. Catharines. Civil defence literature has been handed out by I.O.D.E. volunteers in several larger stores in the district. The director himself has addressed 56 meetings of service clubs, veterans clubs, home and school associations, church groups and parent-teachers groups.
Great care must be taken in the selection of suitable personnel for key positions. As an example, Mr. Joseph Bishop, who had had considerable experience in demolition clearance in England during the war, was given complete charge of this branch of the work. A medical man was given charge of the emergency and ambulance branch, and so on. The organization is set up on a control system. It provides for a central committee made up of representatives from all the councils of the municipalities concerned. The director, of course, is the head of the organization and he has under his jurisdiction three deputy directors:	deputy director G
in charge of intelligence, deputy director A in charge of personnel and administration, and deputy director Q in charge of supply, equipment, transport and buildings. These men, in co-operation with the fire-fighting group, the police group and the rescue group are able to provide a nucleus for a great service in our community.
A bimonthly civil defence newsletter is sent out to all civil defence personnel. Those newsletters are well worth reading. There are approximately 2,200 in the organization who are receiving weekly training. It is difficult to obtain trained instructors and suitable accommodation. Several of our outstanding citizens have taken advantage of

Supply-Health and Welfare the excellent courses provided by the Department of National Health and Welfare both here and at the new school in Arnprior. I am informed by these people who have become prominent and efficient leaders that the courses which they have received have provided them with excellent experience in this type of work.
The city of St. Catharines has turned over one of the unused city schools as a headquarters for civil defence activities. In this building equipment is stored and classes of instruction are carried out each week. The director has held 198 conferences for local civil defence key personnel in order to explain their responsibilities and duties and to discuss methods of procedure.
It is interesting to note that the federal and provincial governments have agreed to pay compensation to enrolled members of civil defence organizations who might be injured or maimed during their course of instruction or training.
Excellent progress has been made in organizing civil defence in St. Catharines and district schools. A co-ordinator and two deputies have been appointed. They work in conjunction with the principals aDd teachers in the schools, both public and separate, and they are providing each day drills for the children of the city in order that they might be made aware of what they ought to do should an attack come.
Each year the St. Catharines civil defence organization enters into a joint scheme with Niagara Falls, Ontario; Niagara Falls, New York; and other border communities in order that they may carry on a joint evacuation in the whole Niagara frontier. The effort last year held in October was most successful. It is anticipated that better results will be achieved when the Niagara Falls, N.Y., exercise is held this coming October.
What is the cost of this program? I believe it is important that I should say something about the cost to local municipalities. The total budget for the areas engaged in this work amounts to $6,291.11. It is distributed among their local municipalities as follows: Distribution of Civil Defence Budget

This is the effort that is being made by the municipalities throughout the county of Lincoln. I think it is a good record. I think it is probably a better record than that of some other parts of Canada. I am hopeful that some scheme may yet be devised between the province of Ontario and the federal government in order that the municipalities in our community may avail themselves of the opportunity to obtain from the federal government some grant to assist them in this type of work.
Why is it so difficult to organize civil defence in Ontario and throughout Canada? The first reason is that none of our cities have ever suffered a really serious actual disaster. The second reason is that Ontario, being far removed from both seacoasts, has not been seriously threatened by war for nearly 150 years. These reasons must be blamed for much of the public apathy that exists at the present time. However, I believe that I have pointed out tonight that given the proper leadership, maintained by adequate municipal support and the encouragement and assistance of the Department of National Health and Welfare, any community can build for itself an adequate measure of protection for its citizens who may be under severe stress and heavy attack.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest to the constructive and interesting remarks of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. I think he made a most interesting contribution to this debate. I listened with interest to the speaker who has just resumed his seat, particularly because he emphasized one aspect of civil defence that has been very much in my mind in recent years. I have taken an interest in the subject ever since civil defence was organized. I have kept in close contact with the officials of the various municipalities in my riding, the civil defence co-ordinators, the fire chiefs and other interested people in local groups, and I have had an opportunity to discuss the varying and changing problems with these people.
I must say I represent a constituency that, relatively speaking, is very well organized for civil defence. As a matter of fact the province of British Columbia is, relatively speaking, well organized for civil defence, particularly when you realize that 2-5 per cent of the total population of the province is enrolled in the civil defence organization at this time. But we have even beaten that in Kootenay West. I have one community, Kinnaird, in which 10 per cent of the total population are enrolled in the civil defence organization.

I think the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich hit the nail on the head when he said that this is the result of neighbourly co-operation. In fairness to those who live in larger centres, I think I should say that I have found from experience in all types of community activity that it is much easier to get neighbourly community co-operation in a small community than in a large city because in a small community each person who is a member of the organization or unit feels that they are wanted, that they are someone important and are doing an effective job.
I quite realize that city conditions present a greater problem to the organization of civil defence than small communities. As far as Kootenay West is concerned, the whole idea of organizing civil defence has been to organize it to meet any form of disaster. We recognize the necessity for civil defence to meet the possibility of disaster from attack. We have dealt with the question of floods on the Columbia and Kootenay rivers, the possibility of having to deal with large fires and with forest fires. Only within the last month or two it was anticipated for some two or three weeks that the Columbia river might rise and seriously flood a portion of the city of Trail and other communities. I may say that the whole civil defence organization was ready to go into action at a moment's notice to build dikes and provide the things required to protect the city of Trail and other communities against the possible flooding of the Columbia and other rivers.
I must repeat again that for civil defence to be successful the first necessity is that it must be based on local interest, local organization and local co-operation. In my district in all the municipalities the great majority of local organizations such as the Red Cross, the Legion, trade unions, fire brigades and so on, the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, the West Kootenay Power and Light Company, all the large logging companies and their employees have worked together through elected representatives to build a foundation for a very successful civil defence organization under excellent local leadership. I have definitely come to the conclusion that no federal or provincial action with respect to civil defence can be successful unless you have that sort of co-operation at the local or rank and file level. That is the reason for the measure of success that has been attained in the district I represent.
Before passing on, I want to pay particular tribute to Major Matheson, who was the co-ordinator in the Nelson area covering the greater part of Kootenay West and the small
Supply-Health and Welfare communities, and to Mr. Marcolin, of Trail, who is the co-ordinator for, you might say, the target area of my constituency. They have both done excellent work in dealing with the questions of evacuation, rescue, medical attention, transportation, communication, organization of food supplies and reception areas. Every outlying village in my district has been visited. There are local committees. Every house, every hall, every building capable of receiving people has been listed. Even my own little log shack is going to be used in case of necessity. All the local fire brigades are taking an active part in this organization.
Earlier in the debate I heard some reference to hose standardization. Hose standardization has been in effect in British Columbia and Alberta as a result of the provincial governments concerned accepting their responsibility in that respect. So far as the question of hose standardization in British Columbia is concerned, it was the fire chief of the city of Nelson who first emphasized that at the first meetings held in Vancouver when the civil defence organization was formed. A number of our active workers in civil defence have attended the civil defence school in Ottawa. They have come down here over a period of two or three years and all of them tell me that they were very pleased with the training and experience and that they thought the training, experience and information they received were most useful and beneficial.
But now we meet a new situation. As the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich said, we need to take a new look at civil defence, and that is recognized by all these lo.cal groups that are doing such good work. I think recent developments require a reexamination of the whole civil defence organization and the measures taken to defend and protect the civil population. In that respect I have seen editorials in many newspapers, and I should like to quote a paragraph from one that appeared in the Citizen of April 12 headed "Civil Defence in the H-Bomb Age". It reads in part as follows:
Civil defence plans are everywhere undergoing a re-examination as a result of the H-bomb explosions in the Pacific. Although discouragement was the first reaction, second thoughts confirm the importance of continued efforts to prepare for disaster. Plans must, of course, be adapted to the possibility of destruction more terrible than the atomic bomb could produce.
I think that reaction to recent developments must be met by the federal government and those responsible at senior levels by some guidance, some instruction and, shall I say, some new leadership. I was particularly interested in the remarks of the

Supply-Health and Welfare hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich with respect to this suggestion that we should have a civil defence act. I had not considered the question before but it seems to have a great deal of merit. Having thought it over since the hon. member spoke, it is my opinion that federal civil defence legislation will dissipate the amorphous situation that exists to some extent at the present time in the administration of civil defence throughout the country.
I hope the minister will give close attention to that suggestion. I also think, in view of the differing financial capabilities of the various governments, that the federal government should reassess the capacity of certain provincial governments to undertake civil defence satisfactorily. Like the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, I do not think it is sufficient to say: If you wish to go into civil defence, we will go along with you and share some of the expense. I think the provincial governments have got to accept their responsibility. That is why I think civil defence legislation would remove somewhat the lack of cohesion that exists today, would define exactly the responsibility of federal, provincial and municipal governments and the people themselves, would provide an opportunity for a definition of the financial responsibilities of all levels of government, and would in general provide the cohesion through legislation that I think is necessary to bring civil defence to the peak of efficiency necessary in Canada at this time.

I should like to say a few
words with respect to the subject under discussion at the present time. I do so because I believe that civil defence is a matter of immediate urgency and grave concern to the people of Canada. Fundamentally civil defence involves the safeguarding of Canadian lives. Since there will be no time, in the event that hostilities and all-out fighting begins, to make preparations, advance preparations are necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Will the hon. member excuse me if I leave the chamber for a few moments?
I shall be right back and I have asked that the hon. member's remarks be followed closely.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Certainly. Advance preparations may well mean the difference between some semblance of morale and ultimate victory and chaos and defeat.
No sane person in the country wants blood spilling. We certainly hope that civil defence will never become a reality in Canada. In the light of what is happening in the world today we have no other recourse except to


take every precaution we possibly can. For those reasons and many more it is regrettable that this important subject, and many of the other controversial matters which are on the agenda at the present time, were not brought up sooner because they certainly justify the full force of debate and the views of every single member in this house.
We notice in the estimates for 1954-55 the vote for civil defence is listed as $6,498,253, which implies a decrease of $8,034 as compared to the amount in the estimates for 1953-54. In comparison with the amounts that are being spent on military defence, I feel that this is but a scratch on the surface of the problem. We read every day in the newspapers of the precarious state of affairs in the world. I personally look upon civil defence measures as being equally as important as military defence. These two precautions certainly cannot be divorced from one another. The urgency of building up our civil defence program is clearly illustrated by statements that appear in our daily newspapers. Here is one that appeared in the Montreal Gazette of June 19, 1954. The heading reads, "Ottawa favours nuclear weapons in any war". It is written by Dave McIntosh, and the article goes on to say:
Canada's defence officials favour-out of necessity-use of nuclear weapons in the event of war.
Further on the article states:
Canada's defence chiefs do not hold any false hopes that the North Atlantic alliance forces in Europe could beat Russia on the ground. NATO forces are considered the barest minimum to hold off a Russian attack long enough for the United States air force and the R.A.F. to swing into action with nuclear weapons and destroy Russia's ability to wage war.
We know that such action could bring counter-strikes upon our own country. In reviewing the present military situation Field Marshal Viscount Montgomery speaking in Paris on May 24 emphasized the urgency of civil defence. The statement appeared in the New York Times of Tuesday, May 25, and reads as follows:
A successful western defence against this threat requires up-to-strength, combat-ready regular army divisions, well-organized reserves, trained and ready to fight, a supply system built in peacetime and ready to roll in war, and sound civil defence and home-front morale.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the urgency of civil defence might best be understood by illustration. There are two facts which I believe are proper to recall at this time. The first fact is that those forces opposed to our way of life are on the offensive. We are on the defensive. They certainly have as their ultimate aim world conquest for communism. Flush with various

diplomatic victories at Geneva and elsewhere, armed with propaganda and great military strength, they now control an area from the river Elbe to the borders of Alaska, an area inhabited by over 800 million people or one out of every three human beings who inhabit this planet.
With some of the south Asian countries unable to defend themselves, perhaps even before we meet again another 500 million human beings may be subjugated. I feel these facts emphasize the urgency of our own military and civil defence preparations. At this rate fragments of Europe and this continent may soon be the only places that are not under communist rule.
The second point I should like to make is that we are still free and unfettered and wish to remain that way. We insist that every precaution be taken, both from a military and civil defence point of view, to safeguard this nation. In order to be effective I believe that civil defence should be conducted on a municipal or community level with as little interference as possible from the central agencies. The matters of co-ordination of defence planning, standardization of defence equipment, guidance and financial cost should be federal responsibilities. This follows the precept that the first responsibility of the federal government is to safeguard the lives and interests of the people. I say this because it seems to me that much of our defence planning has been hampered by argument as to where the financial responsibility lies.
It seems to me we are wasting a great deal of time fiddling on the theme as to who is financially responsible when there is so much to be done and so little time in which to do it. We in the province of Alberta have from the very outset realized the responsibilities which we have in the matter of civil defence. I believe the minister will bear me out when I say that the government of Alberta has given full co-operation in the matter. However, simply because the government of Alberta gives full co-operation in the matter of civil defence should not mean discriminating against our province in the matter of financial assistance or that greater financial inducements be given to those who are less prone to assume their responsibility. A statement of policy from the minister at an early date clarifying the federal government's financial responsibility in this matter will, I believe, clear the decks for quick action and enable the various provinces to expedite those steps which will ensure some degree of safety for their people.
Supply-Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the position of this group was set forth capably on Saturday by my seatmate, the hon. member for Cape Breton South. He pointed out that we are opposed to any suggestion that control of civil defence should be vested in the military authorities or in the Department of National Defence. Rather, we think it should remain where it is, in the civilian department. We urge that the minister be given more authority either by legislation or by agreement with the provinces in order that he may be in a better position to seek co-operation and to assist in the co-ordination of the efforts of provincial and municipal groups in this matter.
In the third place we believe that the minister should have a much larger budget for civil defence than the one presented to us tonight. Yesterday we voted close to $2 billion for national defence; this afternoon we voted $40 million for defence production, and tonight we are asked to vote about $6,500,000 for civil defence. The contrast between these figures is, I think, some indication of the fact that the government itself does not take this matter of civil defence very seriously. Certain it is that it is not taken seriously in the part of Ontario from which I come. The metropolitan areas of this province just do not take civil defence seriously.
There is a great dearth of enthusiasm in the subject, I think partly because our people just cannot grasp the fact that an invasion and destruction of our country or our metropolitan areas is now possible. I do not think the serious threat to our country and indeed to civilization is realized by our people.
In the second place there is very little confidence that much can be done by way of civil defence to protect us from destruction by the hydrogen bomb. There is a dearth of information regarding just what is being done or what can be done. And there is I think a lack of confidence in the present civil defence program to meet the kind of emergency that we would be called upon to meet in case of invasion.
We continue to debate our constitutional rights; whether the federal government, the provinces or municipal bodies should accept the responsibility. We continue to quarrel about the division of costs, as to who should pay this and who should pay that. Meantime I think that we should either take this question seriously or forget about it altogether.
If we are to take it seriously, then I think it is necessary that agreement be reached with the provincial authorities whereby more power can be vested in the federal minister

Supply-Health and Welfare in charge of this department, in order that we may really get on with the job of building up a civil defence organization across this country. And certainly the government should consider spending more money than is asked in this vote for that purpose. The amount of almost $6,500,000 we are asked to vote tonight is to be spent in this way: $2 million for administration, $2 million for grants in aid to the provinces, and $2,400,000 for materials and supplies.
As has been indicated already, a successful civil defence organization depends upon the co-operation of community groups and of provincial governments. But certainly the leadership for the development of a national civil defence organization must of necessity come from the federal department in charge. I think the provinces have some reason to disagree with the terms under which grants in aid are made. After all, in the event of invasion, and of our having to avail ourselves of our civil defence organization, of necessity most of the services and of the personnel will be supplied by the municipalities. In their personnel, in their local organization, in their hospitals and in their police forces as well as their fire departments, the provinces and municipalities have the nucleus of what eventually must become the main part of the local civil defence organization.
In the light of the provisions already made by local and provincial authorities, if the federal government is to take the matter of civil defence seriously and is anxious to see a strong organization built up across this country, then the federal government should reconsider the terms on which this paltry $2 million in grants in aid to the provinces is made. The federal government must come to realize that this is a much more serious business than it seems to realize. It demands of that government a much larger share of the cost of organizing such a defence.
If we can build and organize a system of national civil defence, even though we may never be called upon to use that system, the very fact that in building such an organization we have been able to bring local communities together in a co-operative effort, and to co-operate in a common purpose to have facilities for the benefit of the community itself, means that we shall have achieved a purpose that in my opinion will be well worth the expenditure of money and effort put into it. Even though we are never called upon to use the organization for the purpose for which it was intended, an organization of that kind will, by the very fact that it is brought into the various communities and has enlisted the services in

that community into co-operative enterprise, have made a big contribution to our democratic way of life.
In concluding these remarks, Mr. Chairman, I say that we shall oppose any suggestion that the Department of National Defence should take over civil defence. We shall support any move made to secure cooperation and agreement with the provinces by which more authority can be vested in the minister for the purpose of co-ordinating the efforts of the communities and the provinces across this country in the matter of civil defence. We urge that the federal government take this entire matter of civil defence much more closely into consideration and that a larger budget than the present be provided.
