speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the statement has frequently been made that military spending and preparations for a coming war were always made for the war just past; that is, that they were one war behind. However true that may have been as far as military planning is concerned-I do not think it was true to any great extent in many instances-it is certainly true so far as civil defence is concerned in Canada at the present time. In other words, the activities which have been carried on in civil defence in Canada have been ones really based on experience secured in Great Britain during the last war, and based to a large extent on the concept of the ordinary type of bombs and the problems attendant upon bombing of that kind.
To a large extent the responsibility for civil defence has been passed on to the provinces and to the municipal authorities, and the hope has been that they, with voluntary assistance from the general population, would get an organization set up which would be adequate to look after civil defence matters. That is all very well in its way, but in the atomic age I do not think it is anything like sufficient.
It has been indicated by several of the speakers who preceded me that something much more definite and much more dynamic needs to be done, much better leadership needs to be given and more finances provided by the dominion government in order to provide anything in the way of an effective civil defence. I have nothing against what has been done up to date. The emphasis so far has been on fire fighting, the provision of fire fighting equipment, the standardization of hose couplings and things along that line, rescue work and organization in cities for that rescue work, first aid and the provision of first aid classes for voluntary workers and

so on. That is all good. That is all still necessary; it will all be needed and it can all be made use of. But a great deal more is necessary if we are to have anything in the nature of an effective civil defence organization set up in Canada to meet an atomic bomb attack.
If we are in earnest about this thing, if we believe at all that we are likely to have need of the civil defence organizations; in other words, if we believe there is going to be an attack on Canada, we must predicate our thinking on the basis that it is likely to be an atomic attack so far as certain big concentrations of population and industry are concerned.
To have any sort of realistic civil defence organization, it must be based on that predication; otherwise we might just as well do practically nothing about it. If we accept that premise which is, as far as I can see, the only one we can accept, then I think we have got to accept the fact that much more important than this fire fighting, this rescue work and the first aid is going to be the evacuation of those large centres of population and the finding of places for the people that have to be sheltered, fed and so forth. In other words the whole concept of civil defence really has to be sighted in that direction rather than sighted in the direction of fire fighting in a particular locality, rescue work there and the taking of people from houses that have been bombed to a neighbouring house, and so forth.
If you have an atomic bomb attack on Toronto, for example, you are going to have the entire city of Toronto unfit for human habitation as a result of radioactivity, because most of the buildings will be destroyed or badly damaged, and they are not going to be fit for occupancy. There you will have on your hands the problem of evacuating, if possible. If you have warning you are going to evacuate as many people from those areas as possible before the attack takes place. We would hope that a large number would be evacuated before the attack takes place, but after it does take place the people who have survived would have to be evacuated from that area.
Any realistic civil defence planning must have in mind places where these people can go; therefore it seems to me there are four things in particular which are the essential needs in civil defence planning at the present time and in civil defence plants. The first is the evacuation of people of the larger centres of population, the ones that are likely targets. An evacuation plan of course involves 83276-411J
Supply-Health and Welfare the matter of the use of all available transportation, traffic control and so on, and of course places to which these people can go.
In certain provinces, for example, such as the province of New Brunswick, I do not think there would be any problem if you had to evacuate the only two cities that would perhaps ever have to be evacuated there, namely, Saint John and Moncton. There would be no problem in finding sufficient places for the people from those cities in towns and villages and on the farms in the province of New Brunswick. You have not much of a problem there; it is just a matter of making the plans and then seeing that a sufficient number of people know about them so that they can be carried out.
But when you come to the central provinces of Quebec and Ontario, and particularly Montreal and Toronto, you have a terrific problem on your hands. After you succeeded in evacuating all the population from these two cities where would you put them? There is just not enough room in the form of houses, summer cottages and everything else to put that large number of people. There would not be enough room to accommodate the people who were not destroyed in the blast, if that took place. Therefore, some provision has to be made for these people to go to if an evacuation ever becomes necessary.
A great deal of course can be done in the utilization of farm buildings, summer cottages and things of that sort as temporary shelters, but it seems to me another essential at the present time is the provision of a considerable amount of tentage, places as storehouses or whatever you wish to call it in strategic areas around the country. Fortunately in this country we have provinces which have a large number of lakes that have summer cottages around them and quite a lot of amenities. The provision of water is already there, and so on. This would be the sort of place, I would think, where there should be dumps of tents that could be made use of to make what in wartime we called an emergency town around what is at the present time a comparatively small summer resort. As far as I know nothing along that line has been done. I think that is one of the essentials in any civil defence plan at the present time.
It is no good of course to put these people out in these various areas north of Toronto, Montreal and so forth, unless there is something to eat when they get there. Therefore, in addition to the provision of tentage, we need to have dumps or storehouses of food, food, of course, which can be kept for long periods, such as flour, canned meats, concentrated foods of various sorts, necessities

Supply-Health and Welfare at least, so that the necessities of life can be provided for the people that would evacuate to those areas. I refer to something that would correspond to some extent to the iron rations, as they were called, that were carried by every soldier during the last war and the war before, only of course on a much bigger scale.
The fourth essential is the provision of medical supplies for the treatment of numerous casualties likely to require treatment in these evacuation areas. This is one thing on which I know something has already been done. Provision has been made for a certain number of medical kits and a start has been made in that direction, but as far as I know it is just a start and it is not even close to approaching the needs or necessities of the situation. I understand these medical kits consist of surgical operating instruments, but to my mind what is even more necessary is the provision of drugs, particularly those types necessary in the treatment of burns, radiation, and that sort of thing.
I do not want to take up a great deal of the time of the committee in going into these various points in detail. One could make a ten or fifteen minute speech on each of the four points I have mentioned, namely, evacuation plans, the provision of tenting, the provision of food in dumps, and the provision of medical supplies in dumps. However, for the moment I have touched on what I consider to be the crux of the matter as far as civil defence is concerned, and I would like to hear from the minister as to what progress, if any, has been made along the lines I have mentioned. In other words, what steps have been taken to meet a likely atomic attack rather than the type of planning we have had up to date which was adopted really to meet an ordinary bomb attack?

Mr. Chairman, before the minister answers I would like to make one or two brief comments. I would like to say in the first place that the speech to which we have just listened strikes me as much the most practical approach to this question I have ever heard. What I want to do is merely to underline one or two of the things which have been said and which really are, as it were, background material to this problem. In the first place I must say I agree fully with what the hon. member for York South said, namely that either we should take this very seriously or forget about it altogether. Secondly, I should like to underline what the hon. member for Edmonton East said to the effect that the


matter was one of immediate urgency and great concern to the people of Canada. If he had said it should be a matter of great urgency and immediate concern I would agree with him fully, but I would like to question whether in fact it is a matter of great urgency and immediate concern to one out of a hundred people in Canada. That seems to be the trouble.
I listened with great interest and some amazement to the speech made by the hon. member for Lincoln and if the situation in Lincoln is as he described it then I think we should congratulate him. I was surprised when he mentioned that 163,000 people had been enrolled in the civil defence organizations and I hope the minister when he comes to speak will tell us more about that. It seems to me the job the government has to do is a very difficult one and it has not even been scratched as yet nor have the people of Canada yet been made conscious of this problem. If I am terribly ignorant of the facts and if the people in the part of Canada in which I live are the only ones who are asleep and doing nothing to look after themselves I will be ready to be set right on it, but at the moment it seems to me, as the hon. member for York South pointed out, that we are doing neither one thing or the other. We seem to be like the city fathers of Coventry who decided it was not worth doing anything about civil defence. I believe Sir Winston Churchill answered them, though I do not know how effectively.
I think the problem is one of tremendous difficulty and in spite of the figures mentioned by the hon. member for Lincoln the problem has not even been scratched as yet because the ordinary citizen of Canada is not prepared to do anything about it. It is something about which he does not like to think, and will not think about, and I hope that when the minister comes to answer he will give us a good deal of information. I hope the minister will be utterly realistic about it and tell us the true situation, however unpalatable the truth may be. The minister has a job to do. In his spare time he is supposed to deal with these matters which are of tremendous importance. If we had a bombing attack tomorrow the minister would be grievously and very unfairly blamed for what would be the fault of us all, and I suggest therefore that we be given a very realistic appreciation of this situation as it is and not as we would like it to be.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think all of the
speeches given tonight have been very helpful and I will begin by dealing with the

speech made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South last week and that made tonight by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. I cannot find much to quarrel with in most of the speeches given tonight. As the hon. member for Greenwood has just stated, this is a very difficult matter and anyone who is charged with this particular responsibility has indeed a thankless and very difficult task.
I was interested and encouraged by the observations of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, particularly when he said that since our debate last year he had noted that very considerable progress had been made in the matter of civil defence in Canada. The credit for that does not rest with any particular group but is the result I think of the large measure of co-operation that exists throughout the country and which is greater than is generally appreciated.
Having noted some progress, I fully agree with the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich that the nature of the problem, apart altogether from the assessment of its immediacy, is precisely as he stated. We cannot sit back and say the progress is entirely satisfactory, because it is not satisfactory. It is not satisfactory here nor is it satisfactory in any country in the world. The British home secretary, Sir David Maxwell Fyfe, in the British House of Commons found himself faced with the same kind of questions that have attended the debate here tonight, and the remark which the British Prime Minister, Sir Winston Churchill, made with regard to the attitude taken by some citizens of Coventry is a valid response which we can all make I think to anyone in Canada who claims that civil defence has now been made obsolete as a result of thermonuclear developments. I know of no responsible group in Canada that has taken that position.
The hon. member for Calgary North, in his constructive speech, outlined the steps he thought should be taken in the light of the development of the hydrogen bomb and the four new phases which might be given consideration at this time. He mentioned evacuation and I might associate with that what is evacuation in principle but what is called tactical dispersal of population. The hydrogen bomb has forced us to give consideration to evacuation and tactical dispersal of population.
The hon. member urged that a committee be set up to consider plans with respect to this matter. I would point out that that has been done. We not only have a departmental committee but we have a committee on which the
Supply-Health and Welfare United States and Great Britain share membership with our Canadian representatives. That matter is being carefully studied but it would not be accurate to say that we have yet formulated the kind of plans originally projected as necessary following the first hydrogen detonation. As soon as the first, hydrogen bomb was exploded we were told there were detailed plans already worked out for the evacuation of cities such as New York, but I can say that that is not the case. However, in the United States, Great Britain and in Canada these matters are being given consideration. We hope in Canada in the fall to be able to test out the evacuation plan of one Canadian community yet to be announced.
With regard to medical supplies, my hon. friend referred to surgical kits. Of course our stockpiling program is much more extensive than that. To date we have spent almost $2,500,000 on medical supplies which include drugs, instruments and the sort of thing my hon. friend mentioned; blankets and much else besides, and these are being placed in strategic areas in the country. The matter of tents, and other emergency shelter accommodation, of course is one that is closely related to the question of evacuation and comes within the responsibility of mutual aid and reception areas, as was so helpfully outlined by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. For 3J years now we have had an expert committee studying the question of food supplies and emergency feeding arrangements in the event of the kind of disaster occurring which we all hope will not take place.
One of the encouraging things in this debate tonight, it seems to me, has been the recognition of the fact that civil defence, in order to be effective-apart altogether from what the central and provincial governments must do-depends in the final analysis for its success on the voluntary effort of the Canadian citizen in his or her community. We started civil defence in Canada, as was done in the United States, on the basis of the experience of Great Britain. We have consistently used the services of their officers and notably those of Sir John Hodsoll who had charge of civil defence in Britain during the war and who kept emphasizing the importance, notwithstanding the difficulty, of bringing home so far as possible the necessity for local community organization and of recognizing that there in the main rested the secret of the

6SC0
Supply-Health and Welfare success of an adequate civil defence organization. This fact was recognized also in the United States when President Eisenhower in February of this year said:
Civil defence responsibilities primarily belong to the state and local governments-recruiting, training and organizing volunteers to meet any emergency. The immediate job of the federal government ... is to supply technical guidance, and to continue to strengthen its civil defence stockpile of medical, engineering and related supplies and equipment.
Again, in his budget statement a few months ago-and this is an important statement-he said this:
Much planning, organization, and training remains to be done, however, to make this strategy of civil defence fully effective at all levels of government. It will be the federal responsibility, as reflected in this budget, to provide warning of impending attacks, and to stockpile medical supplies. The federal government will not assume the responsibilities which belong to local governments and volunteer forces, but will supplement state and local resources, provide necessary information on weapons' effects, and advise and assist states and localities . . .
This great problem is really outside the realm of money and material preparation. Its solution is in conviction and belief, in readiness and discipline- in those things that need to be done by the population to save itself.
That represents our view and that is equally the view of Her Majesty's government in the United Kingdom.
Before I announce our financial arrangements pursuant to a recent dominion-provincial conference I should like to say this in view of what was said here tonight by one or two members. There has been the fullest co-operation between the two senior levels of government. I do not say that every province has agreed with the decision we have taken. One province, namely the province of Quebec, has co-operated by coming to the meetings and has taken its part in our planning at the centre. It has acted as the distributing agency for much educational material which we have provided. But it has taken the position that it does not propose to spend any of its own money in assisting municipalities in the matter of civil defence.
In the province of Ontario, the provincial government there took the position that the new formula which I am going to refer to in a few moments was one to which they could not accede. They did not propose to make any grants themselves to any municipalities. By way of parentheses I should explain that under the present financial arrangement we are not able to make any grants direct to the municipalities unless the province also makes a grant. The result is that certain municipalities who have their own budget and who have been carrying on without provincial help have for that reason not been receiving any direct assistance from the federal government.

In the case of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, they have not been receiving any money from the provincial governments. Nevertheless, in the province of Ontario no one should conclude that that province is not concerning itself seriously with civil defence. We may have our differences of opinion. That is natural with any group. We may have our differences of opinion as to whether a particular effort is more desirable than another. But in the province of Ontario there are over 200 communities which have a civil defence organization in various stages of development.
The hon. member for Lincoln tonight referred to his own city of St. Catharines. He was perfectly justified in doing so because it is a most outstanding example. In that community there are 2,200 civil defence workers. The community provides its own budget. Their civil defence director, who works at the job day and night, is doing so on a voluntary basis. The result of his efforts is seen in the picture which the hon. member for Lincoln so ably outlined tonight.
In Ontario the provincial government has taken the position that at this time it does not propose to make grants to the municipalities directly. I am sure however that it would be prepared to accept moneys from the federal government to assist the municipalities. Incidentally about $250,000 is now being spent in the province of Ontario. Most of that money is being spent in a program of standardization of hose couplings-a program costing over $1 million-to which the federal government has contributed roughly one-third. A program of standardization of hose couplings is, of course, an extremely important item in the development of a civil defence program. In addition to that, they have an administrative budget which provides for the services of their administrator who said the other day in Sudbury that just as soon as Ontario's standardization of hose couplings program has been completed, it is the hope that Ontario will give consideration to further provincial funds being made available in support of civil defence.
I should like to say that within the past ten days I have had a chat with the premier of the province of Ontario. From my conversation with him I am satisfied that we shall be able to work out, within the formula to which I shall later refer, a satisfactory arrangement supplemental to that now being carried on in the province of Ontario. It is wrong to assume that the only kind of assistance the federal government has given to the provinces with regard to civil defence is in the matter of matching grants.

The only matching grants that exist thus far represent a sum of about $1,400,000. The rest of the expenditures last year, provision for sirens, provision for certain civil defence equipment, civil defence clothing and all that sort of thing, represents not a grant to the municipalities or provinces on a matching basis but an outright grant paid entirely by the federal government. For instance, there is no matching provision with respect to our civil defence school at Arnprior. We have trained over 4,000 individuals there who have come from all over Canada at federal expense and have been maintained in the college at federal expense. The 4,000 people trained in that college, now under the direction of General Penhale, have provided among others the civil defence co-ordinators throughout the country. These in turn have trained another 40,000 people.
That represents a very substantial contribution entirely by the federal government. Then there is the matter of films, pamphlets and folders. All that sort of thing is done entirely by the federal government, and these things are given to the provinces as the distributing agencies. When civil defence was established in Canada it was done on the basis that this was a federal state and that we had to work with the provinces. That was what the provinces wanted; that is what the provinces want today. In each province there is a civil defence minister. He is the agent through whom we address ourselves to the municipalities, and it seems to me, having in mind the character of civil defence in Canada, that is the kind of pattern we should follow.
In the fiscal year 1954-55 we propose, in addition to the things the federal government does for which it pays 100 per cent and which represent more than two-thirds of the federal expenditure, to make available $2 million which will be available to the provinces and the municipalities under the matching grant program for approved civil defence projects. To indicate the distribution of these grants to the provinces perhaps I might be allowed to put on Hansard, a statement showing what this will mean to each province compared with the moneys made available to them in 1953-54. May I have the permission of the committee to have these figures put on Hansard?

In order to ensure the most effective utilization of these funds, an entirely new formula has been worked out in co-operation with the provinces, and as the result of a dominion-provincial conference held in this building about two weeks ago. This formula will permit federal aid to municipalities undertaking civil defence projects, regardless of whether or not provincial assistance is available. The federal grant to municipalities, however, can be increased up to double the basic amount for any project for which provincial aid is also available.
Under the revised formula of civil defence expenditures will be broken down into the following six classifications;
1.	Organization and administration.
2.	Training, equipment and operations.
3.	Warning communications and other civil defence equipment for which there is no peacetime use.
4.	Construction for civil defence purposes such as control centres.
5.	Civil defence operational equipment having a peacetime use.
6.	Purchase of clothing, including uniforms, for civil defence workers.
As a matter of policy, not more than one-quarter of the total provincial quota will normally be allocated to any one of the six

Supply-Health and Welfare main divisions of civil defence expenditure. This, we hope, will have the effect of developing a well advanced and well balanced program. For projects falling within the first four expenditure groups, which include civil defence services having no direct peacetime application, the federal government will contribute a minimum of 25 per cent of the cost of any approved project regardless of whether a provincial grant is made. In addition, the federal government will also match any provincial contribution to the same project up to an over-all maximum of 50 per cent of the total cost. Thus, for projects supported by all three governments, the costs will be shared as follows: 50 per cent by the federal government, 25 per cent by the provincial government and 25 per cent by the municipal government.
That, basically, is the pattern of assistance given civil defence operations by the central government in Great Britain to the municipal bodies in the United Kingdom. For expenditures falling within the last two classifications, those having a peacetime value, the arrangements will be the same as in the past. The federal government in that case will match dollar for dollar any provincial contributions.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich noted progress over last year and I am sure he would want me to supplement that by noting that our 1954-55 budget for civil defence, $6,500,000, is more than five times the combined budgets of the provincial governments which total $848,000 and the twenty-two municipal corporate target areas which represent a total of $386,000. Total provincial and municipal expenses to date represent a figure of about $1,234,000.
The hon. member for Greenwood said to me that I should tell the house the situation exactly as we see it, and that is what I am seeking to do. Before I take my seat, I wish to state that within the past month we have asked the provincial authorities to give us their latest figures on the extent of civil defence organization throughout the country. All of them have reported to us, and the figure totals some 163,000 individuals in 600 different communities, in varying phases of organization, undoubtedly some good, some not as good and some that cannot be commended at all.
I think I can say in fairness, because I am close to the situation in the United States through being a member of the United States-Canadian committee, and because of what Sir John Hodsoll has said, that this is comparable to the United Kingdom and is better than the United States. In terms of contributions, our financial contributions represent roughly 47 cents per

capita whereas those of the United States represent roughly 29 cents per capita. Therefore I think I can say in all honesty that we are building what the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich said was our role now, a nuclear organization in as many areas of the country as we think that should be done. We are providing the basic organization. I am sure that at this time we could get more people to enrol. We could have more excitement, more agitation. We could do what they do in some other places, have signs in hotels and all that sort of thing indicating extraordinary activity.
We have decided that the course that we are taking is the wisest course. It is based upon our assessment of the likelihood of the danger. We could be wrong and, as the hon. member for Greenwood said, if we were wrong I would certainly be the individual who would feel the consequences of that error more than anyone else. I can only say that I feel we are proceeding on the right basis. I feel that what has been said here tonight will help us greatly in the continued difficult task which is ours in co-operation with all provinces and municipalities, the task of building up a practical, sensible organization which will be capable of effective operation when needed.

Whatever may be said in any other country, let us deal with Canada. Here in the city of Ottawa there might be some of us who might have

No one surely would suggest that there is any similarity or that there is not a great difference between the nature of the civil


defence program that might be regarded as desirable in some of the cities such as No-randa, Sudbury, Niagara Falls, Trail, Kitimat and Arvida, as compared with other cities of the same size, perhaps, but without any similarly so far as a target would be concerned. Why should those municipalities be shouldered with a very special responsibility of organizing their civil defence and paying for it; or why should the province whose finances are also limited be called upon to pay for those special arrangements?
No, this situation has no reality; and it is not comparable most certainly in any way to the situation in the United Kingdom under their civil defence act which lays down plans for the period of what we hope will be continuing peace, but which also lays down detailed plans to meet the eventuality for which the act is designed if, unhappily, civil defence should have to be used.
The minister is well aware that neither the government of Ontario nor the government of Quebec nor the governments of the other provinces agree with the proposals that have been put forward. And there have been positive proposals put before this government; and I would like to indicate what they are. I suggest they are worthy of consideration by this House of Commons, and that something should be incorporated in a civil defence act passed by the House of Commons and the parliament of Canada which would deal effectively with them.
One of the important things is of course the recruitment of personnel. The recruitment of personnel involves expense. The more vulnerable targets such as an aluminum centre, a power centre, a nickel centre or automobile centres such as Oshawa and Windsor, or any other centre that has a high war potential or defence potential, would be called upon to make more than ordinary preparations. Specially high recruitment calls for intense organization.
One of the suggestions made was that for every registered member of a local civil defence organization there should be a specific grant by the federal government that would relate directly to the number of registered and trained civil defence workers. It would have a sense of reality in relation to the needs of the particular communities, depending upon their strategic significance.
Another point that was greatly emphasized was the importance of abandoning large defence buildings, or large defence centres. In fact the contention has been made-and I believe it is sound-that it is unwise to spend money on civil defence headquarters located right in the centre of communities,

because when those communities become targets the whole civil defence structure would be paralysed right away. Emphasis has been placed upon the desirability of having the organization apart from the perimeter of target areas.
In fact the argument has been put forward that there be fire-fighting equipment with flexible mobile units also operating from the perimeter of threatened areas, so that in the event of threatened areas becoming targets in an area they could be served by such mobile units. This would follow the plan in operation in the United Kingdom at this time.
Also there is the tremendous need emphasized by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich for those who are trained in the handling of crowds, who are trained in organized plans for evacuation, and for the handling of traffic under pressure. Those who have seen from the air the crowds which attend the running of the Queen's Plate, or similar events in other parts of Canada, will realize that there are those who are called upon to specialize in that particular type of traffic organization.
Then, fire and panic are two of the most serious considerations. Panic is not the least of these, as is so tragically portrayed with such terrible realism in this book to which I have referred.
Surveys of roads should be made under the authority of the federal government. Such a survey of roads should not be a superficial matter; it should be a definite, positive and complete survey, with pickets allotted and stationed at key points along those roads to deal with the results of fire and the possibility of panic or overcrowding on the highway.
Then, there is not merely evacuation, in the sense of moving people, there is also the very real problem of the evacuation of older people, people who are not able to move around themselves.
All this calls for something of a much more central measure of authority than now exists.
I submit that, in their order, fire fighting, traffic control and welfare are the things that need to be brought under some over-all federal plan; by all means with the co-operation of the provinces, by all means with the co-operation of the municipalities, but under an act of parliament that recognizes that this is a national problem.
Again I come back to the question of finances. To do these things the municipalities are simply incapable at this time of shouldering the burdens that would be imposed upon them; so also are the provincial governments.
Supply-Health and Welfare As was said by the Hon. Arthur Welsh, the minister in the Ontario government who is responsible for this matter: Ontario and Quebec are not going to saddle their municipalities with all kinds of new expenditures.
It does not mean a lack of co-operation; it means that they are facing the realities of the problems before them. No one questions the earnestness with which those associated with this work have been carrying on their work. Those who know him personally, as well as those who know him merely by reputation, would have no hesitation in expressing their admiration of the work by General Worthington under extremely difficult circumstances, and under extremely frustrating conditions. I may say that those who know General Penhale will be sure of his ability to perform the tasks that he has been called upon to carry out.

War veterans allowances and other benefits-
517. War veterans allowances, $27,365,500.

Mr. Chairman, this item provides for the payment of war veterans allowances. When the minister dealt with this subject on June 17 he had this to say, as found at page 6195 of Hansard:
I could not see how a major change could be made in this legislation-
He was of course dealing with the war veterans allowance legislation. I continue:
-which would break the ties that have existed between war veterans allowances and old age pensions, a relationship which has always existed between those two pieces of legislation.
That statement by the minister is inaccurate in view of the changes that have been made in the old age pension legislation. I would ask him to clarify how he justifies making the statement that there are those strong ties that have existed between war veterans allowances and old age pensions.
As the committee knows, some years ago the old age pension was changed to old age security, and it is payable automatically without any means test to everyone who reaches the age of 70 years. There is no ceiling


whatever on the earnings or income that a recipient of old age security may have. In view of these changes I wish the minister would explain just what connection there now is between the war veterans allowance and old age security.
I point out to him that in addition to the payment of $40 a month which is made automatically by the dominion government, some of the provincial governments add a supplement. I believe British Columbia and Alberta pay an additional $15 which of course brings the payment to a larger amount than the war veterans allowance recipient gets.
In view of the emphasis the minister places on this fact that there is this very strong tie between the war veterans allowance and the old age pension, I believe that in justice to the veterans of this country he should explain just how he reaches the conclusion that there is such a tie.
Then, with regard to the old age assistance, as distinct from old age security, that assistance is on a means test basis and it is paid at the age of 65. If there is to be any parallel between that type of payment and the war veterans allowance then the latter allowance should be made at the age of 55 instead of 60. Then, the old age assistance is quite unlike old age security for in the former case one-half is paid by the dominion and the other half by the provinces. There is provision for additional payment by some of the provinces. I believe the two provinces I have mentioned, British Columbia and Alberta, bring the old age assistance payment up to $55 a month, subject of course to a means test.
But I have instanced those two types of old age pension, first, the old age security and then the old age assistance, and I wish the minister would explain just what he means when he says that the war veterans allowance must remain tied to the old age pension. In view of the facts I have outlined I think there is very little connection left between payments to the front-line troops and either one of these old age payments.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe there is very little I can add to what I have already said on this particular matter regarding the relationship between the war veterans allowance, and what used to be known as the old age pension, now known as old age assistance, and the old age security payments. In my remarks the other day I mentioned that the history of this relation had been made very clear by the hon. member for Acadia, and I know that the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra is as familiar as I am, if not more so, with the history of war veterans allowance.

I explained the other day, as I have on other occasions, that the war veterans allowance was instituted in an attempt to make available to those who could qualify under the terms of the act the same kind of benefits as a citizen could draw under the Old Age Pensions Act and that ever since the act was instituted in 1930, there has always been a relation between the payments made under the two separate acts. When the amount of the old age pension was raised from $20 to $30 and then $40 the same increases were made in the war veterans allowance, and the ceilings which were incorporated in the acts as regards permissible income have always borne a relation with each other. I think if the hon. member will look up the debate which took place when this act was first brought before parliament he will find I am justified in making this assertion.

This point is of the utmost importance because the minister based his whole case for refusing to give any further consideration to war veterans allowance on the fact that the war veterans allowance must be tied to the old age pension. That is the basis for the government's refusal to do anything about the War Veterans Allowance Act. Now, I have no intention of pursuing the matter further tonight beyond pointing out that when the old age pension was put on an automatic basis it was made payable without a means test to everyone in Canada who reached the age of 70. When that was done that pension no longer had any connection with the war veterans allowance.
Veterans should be treated on an entirely different basis. The claim of those fighting men to war veterans allowance should not be tied down to any old age security payment or old age assistance payment and the whole war veterans allowance picture should be treated on its own merits rather than there being an attempt made to tie it up with the old age pension because it is no longer connected with that; furthermore, as I pointed out the other night, the claim of these men to consideration on the part of the Canadian government rests on far stronger ground than the claim of the civilian because it is based on their willingness to give their lives for their country.

Mr. Chairman, there is no intention on my part to delay the passage of the minister's estimates by repeating arguments already advanced by several of my colleagues. I concur wholly in their observations with respect to the inadequacy of the amount paid. Moreover, I concur in their argument that the income ceilings are altogether too low. I also concur wholly in
Supply-Veterans Affairs the observation made by my colleague the hon. member for Acadia, namely, that when a veteran in receipt of war veterans allowance reaches the age of 60 the means test should be abolished. After all, it is nothing more than a recognition of the principle that the veteran has a prior right at the age of 60.
There are two other matters to which I would like to refer briefly. The first relates to the widows of imperial veterans. Under the regulations as they stand today an imperial veteran resident in Canada for a period of 20 years becomes eligible for the war veterans allowance. Should he die subsequent to the receipt of the war veterans allowance his widow is entitled to an allowance. However, the situation which has come to my attention in my own constituency is that there are a number of imperial veterans, or possibly I should say there were, who died after having resided in Canada for a period of 19 years or 19 years 6 months. Because of the death of that imperial veteran before he established his residential qualification his wife is entirely without benefit. I consider that to be wholly unfair. Had the imperial veteran lived an additional six months or one year he would have qualified and upon his death his wife would have qualified for that benefit. Surely it is only fair and proper that we should recognize the existence of the imperial veteran's widow once she has herself established a 20-year residence in Canada. I urge the minister and the government to give favourable consideration to that particular problem. The mere fact that such cases have come to my attention in my own constituency does not mean that the only widows so affected are in my constituency. There must be a number of them all across Canada.
Secondly, with respect to the amount paid to the recipient of war veterans allowance and the allowable maximum income, I would point out to the minister that there are two types of veterans who are in receipt of this allowance. One is the person who, not being eligible for a pension, should be made eligible for a pension but has not been able to convince the commission that his disability was attributable to war service or aggravated thereby. He may be wholly incapacitated with the result that, if he is a single man, his income is limited to $600 a year. If he is a married man his income is limited to $1,080 a year. But if he is a recipient of war veterans allowance and is not wholly incapacitated, being single he receives $600 a year plus whatever he is able to earn over and above the $600, of course providing that
6508	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs the maximum does not exceed the allowable maximum. I think the government would be justified in establishing a sliding scale of benefits.
Ordinarily I would be hesitant about suggesting that you take recipients of war veterans allowance and put them in two categories. But certainly you are justified in taking the recipient of war veterans allowance who is wholly incapacitated and allowing him more by way of basic allowance than you would allow a man who suffers a 50 per cent or a 25 per cent disability and is able to earn sufficient to bring him up to the total maximum allowable income under the act. I say to the minister that I think the government would be completely justified in establishing a sliding scale of benefits taking into consideration the physical condition of the recipient and also taking into consideration, in the light of his disability, his earning power.
I therefore make this suggestion to the minister. I could take my full 40 minutes in relation to this matter, but I do not intend to do so. Before another session of parliament rolls around I hope the minister and his department and the government will give favourable consideration to the widow of the imperial veteran and to the recipient of war veterans allowance.

521. To provide for payments to the Last Post fund; for the payment under regulations of funeral and cemetery charges; for the cost and erection of headstones in Canada; for the maintenance of departmental cemeteries; for the maintenance of Canadian battlefields memorials in France and Belgium and for Canada's share of the expenditures of the imperial war graves commission, $1,503,400.

I have been waiting for some months to express my thanks to the minister for the courtesy that was extended to me by his officers when I was in Europe last year. Colonel Alan Chambers who was in charge of the D.V.A. office in London was kind enough to make arrangements so that I could visit the Vimy memorial and some of the other cemeteries in France. Those who have not seen the Vimy memorial have missed visiting one of the finest memorials anywhere. It was designed by Walter S. Allward, of Toronto. Those who go to Vimy from all parts of the world have been very kind in the references they have made in the guest book there.
I think a special word of appreciation should be paid to Mr. Paul Piroson and Madame Piroson for the outstanding work they have done in looking after the memorial. I am sure that the relatives of soldiers who were buried in France and in Europe during the first or the second world war would receive a good deal of comfort from visiting any of these cemeteries. I do not know of any cemeteries in Canada that are kept in as good condition as are the cemeteries that I visited last fall. I merely want to thank the minister for the courtesy extended to me

by his officers and to express appreciation tor the outstanding work that is being done there by those who are looking after the cemeteries.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to bring to the minister's attention the fact that I do not think the regulations concerning payments from the Last Post fund are sufficiently publicized. I am repeatedly running into people in the Legion and veterans and their dependents who are not aware of the regulations under which payments are made. I would suggest that something be done to bring again to the attention of Legion branches and people interested the regulations in connection with the Last Post fund and under what conditions payment is made for the burial of the dead.

On May 4 I asked the Minister of Veterans Affairs a question concerning the record of the burial plot for Canadian servicemen buried in war graves overseas. At that time the particular point I raised was that $1.25 was being charged for a copy of the entry in the cemetery and memorial registers which gave details of the plot. The minister indicated that this charge of $1.25 was in payment for pamphlets, books and other printed material issued by the imperial war graves commission to each of the cemeteries in which commonwealth forces are buried. At the time I did not pursue the matter further because I wanted to be sure of the facts.
I have discovered that the charge is not for descriptive pamphlets, books, et cetera, but is for the specific registration of the individual serviceman involved. A prepared form is sent out to the family of the deceased veteran asking them if they would like to pay $1.25 for this specific individual registry which describes the plot record of their member of the family. I am sure the minister has inquiries from time to time concerning the graves overseas.
I know that as a private member of the house I have had several anxious inquiries from constituents who have a loved one buried in one of these war cemeteries overseas. The suggestion has been put forward that some assistance might be given to make it possible for mothers of deceased personnel to make a pilgrimage to the graves of their sons. I do not know whether that suggestion has ever been considered seriously by the department, but it comes to me frequently enough to make me wonder if it is feasible at all. I would suggest that the charge of $1.25 for the individual record is perhaps going a little too far. Members of the families of deceased personnel would like to have the information, and they resent
Supply-Veterans Affairs very much having to pay $1.25 for that record. Has the minister any further comment?

As I mentioned at the time the hon. member brought this question before the house, these books to which the hon. member refers contain not only the names of all ex-servicemen of the commonwealth who may be buried in a particular cemetery. Item agreed to.
Canadian pension commission-[DOT]
523.	Administration expenses, $2,202,908.

This item concerns the pension commission. In reading the report of the Department of Veterans Affairs I was endeavouring to examine the statistics concerning the number of cases that came before the Canadian pension commission, and I found that I had to look at pages 40 and 41, where the veterans bureau reported, and then on pages 69 and 70 where the report of the Canadian pension commission is given. One finds that the figures do not correspond. Might I suggest that these two bodies co-operate in publishing their findings so that there is some relationship between those figures submitted by the two groups. They are both undertaking the same work, and it makes it a little easier for the purpose of one who is investigating if the figures are the same.
I shall give one example. On page 41 appeal board hearings are listed as 1,823, and the Canadian pension commission gives that figure as 1,754. I do not propose to speak at length on this problem, but I should like to repeat what I said earlier this session that I believe the work of the pension commission needs to be reviewed. We have been going on now for years accepting the work of the pension commission without much in the way of criticism. I am not offering any serious criticism at the moment. I believe the work of the commission has been good. I believe the very fact it has been good means that it could stand a detailed review as well as any other department.
The reason I suggest that the work of the Canadian pension commission should be reviewed, and I hope it will be eventually by a standing committee on veterans affairs,

is that I feel some of their work is hindered by limitations in the act. It may be hindered by limitations within the pension commission itself, but I do not know. I prefer to think it is because of the act. The reason I put that forward is that I am rather unfavourably impressed by the number of cases which come before the pension commission and end by being rejected. It seems to me there is a weakness here when cases can be heard on many different occasions. There is the matter of hope deferred for the applicant, then the case finally ends in failure. Of course, that is not always the case. There is a survival rate in these cases that come up for several hearings.
Under the pension commission arrangements first war cases may have a first hearing, then a second hearing, followed by the appeal board. Then, world war II cases may have an initial hearing and then several renewals as follows: first renewal, second renewal, third renewal, further renewal and then appeal. Checking the figures on page 41 of the report, I find that on further renewal-this would be second war cases- eight were allowed by the Canadian pension commission, which means that those eight cases were heard on five different occasions. I am rather surprised that in this sifting process a case that is granted on the fifth hearing should not be granted much earlier.
Then the report shows those that were allowed by the Canadian pension commission, having gone through five hearings, and we find 18 of them were allowed. This does not take into account those which, having passed through three, four or five hearings, are subsequently allowed on appeal. It is for that reason I suggest the work of the pension commission might very well be reviewed. Something might be done to enlarge its function in some way so that the applicants would not be put through all this trouble of hearing after hearing before their cases are finally determined.
One thing that might be investigated in reviewing the work of the pension commission is the length of time that is spent in some of these cases. They must consider them for a very long period indeed. I suggest another reason for reviewing the work of the pension commission and that is to discover in what circumstances the benefit of the doubt clause is used. I have been told it enters into every case but I take that with a grain of salt. I know of instances where, in my opinion, the benefit of the doubt clause should have been invoked and was not. This clause was put into the act for the express purpose, as I understand it, of permitting the pension commission to decide
Supply-Veterans Affairs marginal cases and allowing the benefit of the doubt where the weight of evidence did not seem to be entirely in favour of the applicant. In many cases the weight of the evidence is not in favour of the applicant, and for many reasons, one being that further evidence could not be brought forward. Why could not the work of the pension commission be reviewed with regard to that and if the act needs to be altered, then let it be altered?
I am finishing my remarks now, but I should like the minister to let me know the qualifications for the appointment of a member of the pension commission.

My hon. friend asks what are the qualifications for appointment to the pension commission. As he well knows, there is nothing in the act setting out those qualifications. Generally speaking one requires some experience in dealing with veterans affairs, with veterans legislation, with veterans themselves. In other cases professional experience and qualifications have been essential. That at times has been the case since I have been Minister of Veterans Affairs because it has been necessary to appoint commissioners with medical qualifications, coupled with a knowledge of service conditions and experience in dealing with servicemen. Those were the qualifications upon which these commissioners were appointed. Outside of that, I would say it is left entirely to the judgment of the governor general in council, as specified under the act.

I was wondering, Mr. Chairman, whether in appointing the commissioners there was a balance as between the three services? Is the question of active service considered when it comes to the appointment of a commissioner, as well as the branch of the service with which he served? Does the question of the rank a man has occupied during service enter into consideration at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I know that the three services are represented on the commission. I also know that every one of the commissioners has seen active service in a theatre of war.

I hope the minister will take into consideration some of the things I have already said. Then, I would like to add this, that the pension commission has its own internal appeal board. It may look different from what the facts actually are. I would point out that a person may be turned down by the pension commission and then is permitted an appeal. He discovers that the appeal board consists of three of the commissioners who were not originally on his case.

I think what happens from that arrangement is this, that the commissioners are interchanging their cases. For instance three of them may sit on a case and find against it. Then when it comes up for appeal, three of their colleagues would have to hear that appeal while the first three, in their turn, may be hearing an appeal from the three who are now listening to the case the first three originally tried.
There is this danger within a commission, of a group of colleagues passing cases back and forth among themselves. It might well be worthy of consideration to have an appeal board separate and apart from those who are handling these other cases. Has the minister given consideration to that matter at any time?

Item agreed to.
524.	Pensions for disability and death, including pensions granted under the authority of the civilian government employees (war) compensation order, P.C. 45/8848 of November 22, 1944, which shall be subject to the Pension Act; and including Newfoundland special awards, $128,030,500.

Mr. Chairman, this is the item for the payment of pensions. During the discussion in committee one weakness came to light which I think could be remedied by a regulation. Some years ago a provision was made under which a veteran who had been wounded could have his pension increased automatically by a certain percentage as he reached different ages. But that did not apply to a pensioner who was getting a pension of 80 per cent or over.
In the committee it was explained that the reason the increases stopped with the veteran who was getting an 80 per cent pension or more was that at that time an 80 per cent pension carried with it an automatic pension for the widow, whether the veteran died of his pensionable disability or not.
In order that the widows of those men who had suffered gunshot wounds should not lose out in case a man died from something different, let us say from a disease of one kind or another, this regulation was brought into effect. As the minister knows, a few years ago that 80 per cent line was reduced to 50 per cent, so that the widow of every 50 per cent pensioner would automatically get a pension on his death, no matter what the cause of death might be.
I do suggest that now it would be fair to make this automatic increase apply to the men who have 80 per cent disability or over.
I know for example if a man has his arm off right at the shoulder he cannot get more than 80 per cent, under the present system of assessment, although actually that man as he becomes older is completely disabled. I think


a veteran with a wound of that type should be able to qualify for an automatic increase, just as his comrades could do who started out with a 60 per cent instead of an 80 per cent disability.
I think there has been an oversight in this instance in not having the regulation changed at the time that the automatic protection for the widow was reduced in the case of 80 per cent disability to that of 50 per cent disability. I wonder if the minister would give some thought to that situation during the recess, so that it could be remedied by a regulation or by a change in the method of assessment. As I understand it there is no need to have amending legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I shall be glad most certainly to look into the matter. Of course one would have to consider the purpose of the original regulation. My understanding is that it was given originally for the benefit of the amputees. All these men suffering from gunshot wounds had fixed assessments. A man who had lost his arm at the elbow had a fixed assessment. One who lost his whole arm, or his leg, had a fixed assessment. And as he grew older, although his pensionable disability showed no sign of aggravation- in other words his arm cut off at the elbow was still in the same condition

his general condition, particularly in the case of leg amputees, did deteriorate.
Various conditions were thought to result from an amputation. As he had a fixed assessment of, let us say 60 per cent for the loss of a leg at a certain level, the commission could not increase the disability pension simply in regard to that. To compensate for general deterioration an automatic disability increase was put through in the regulations.
In the case of another sort of disability pensioner, one for instance who might have suffered from a heart condition which was assessed at 30 per cent at the time he was discharged, as the years go by and as his heart condition deteriorates, he returns to the commission and gets a new assessment, which the other man could not obtain. I understand that was the principle which brought about this regulation. However I will be glad to study the point my hon. friend has brought forward.
The difficulty is that a man who had his arm off at the elbow does get an automatic increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

But the man who had it off
at the shoulder does not get that automatic increase, because he was getting an 80 per cent pension at the start. And there was no

provision made for increasing anyone with an 80 per cent pension. But he deserves it just as much as the other chap.
The difficulty was, of course, that the widow of the man who only had his arm off at the elbow could not qualify for pension unless he was getting an 80 per cent pension. Therefore the increases were graduated so that when he got to the top stage he would be getting 80 per cent and his widow would become eligible. But so far as the two men themselves were concerned, the man who had his arm off right at the shoulder does not get any increase at all; he receives no automatic increase.
I do not think that is fair; I think he should receive it. I know of cases where men have that disability and they cannot get more than 80 per cent.

Soldier Settlement and Veterans' Land Act-
526. To provide for the cost of administration of Veterans' Land Act; soldier settlement and British family settlement, $4,907,146.

Mr. Chairman, although I was not a member of the special committee on veterans affairs I did make it a point to read every word of evidence taken before that committee. While perusing the minutes of the proceedings and evidence for Tuesday, May 25, 1954, I came across this rather interesting exchange of questions and answers. I refer to page 138 of the proceedings, where the hon. member for Acadia asked this question:
I would like to ask Mr. Rutherford one question. Can you tell us how the veterans who were settled on government land in the special areas in the so-called "drought area" are getting on? I am especially interested in that because I know you were a little leery in the first instance about settling any veterans in there but finally under pressure from the veterans themselves you did allow a few to settle in there and I understand they are doing very well.
A. I cannot answer that very definitely, Mr. Quelch. There were a few who did not succeed but those who are there now are getting along very well.
Q. About the same percentage of arrears as the rest of Canada?
A. We have more arrears in the Red Deer region.
Naturally that drew my attention very quickly. I continue:
There are only two other regions which have more arrears than Red Deer. I think this report indicates that Dauphin and Grande Prairie have more than Red Deer. It should not be as bad as it is. I believe Mr. Allam has one at Drumheller.
A person seeing and reading that might well come to a wholly erroneous impression. As hon. members know, I represent the Red Deer constituency and have represented that constituency for more than fourteen years.
Supply-Veterans Affairs I have lived in that section of Alberta for a period of twenty-five years. I say without fear of successful contradiction that the Red Deer area is one of the finest mixed farming areas in the whole Dominion of Canada. Settled between Olds and Lacombe are as many if not more veterans settled under V.L.A. than in any comparable area in the Dominion of Canada. I wish to compliment the officials of V.L.A., first for having permitted so many veterans to settle in that area. Second, I wish to compliment them upon exercising a good deal of care in satisfying themselves that the land upon which those veterans were all settled was reasonably good land. Of course I may interject by saying that most of it is, unless you get too far out. But this is a very important thing. We are subjected to natural hazards in that area. We have had some very bad hail years in the Red Deer area. In 1952 many of the farm crops were devastated as a consequence of hail.
I have said in this house before that owing to the regulations under which P.F.A. operates it is extremely difficult for many of the farmers in that area to qualify for P.F.A. benefits. To farm in an area like the Red Deer area is costly, as it is costly in most mixed farming areas. When hail comes along crops are devastated. The individual is faced with the costs involved in the planting of that crop. He is also faced with costs involved in feeding livestock and in procuring seed for the following year.
I know from personal experience two things. The men who are settled under V.L.A. in the Red Deer area are in the main fine types of individuals, anxious to succeed in their chosen occupation. I also pay tribute at this time to the men of V.L.A. in that area who are administering the V.L.A. I know most of those men. I have discussed these matters with them and as one said to me one day, it does seem that for some reason or other the forces of nature pick out these veterans when a hail storm comes through.
I mention that for this reason. I appreciate first the desire of V.L.A. to collect during good years, and we have had some good years. But in assessing good and bad years, for goodness' sake let them not overlook the fact that there may be a bad year in a particular area. In the particular area of Alberta that I represent they have been most unfortunate in the fact that they have had some very bad experiences from the standpoint of hail. I trust that the officials of V.L.A. in Ottawa will pay considerable heed to the advice given to them by the local officials of V.L.A. Do not just simply pick out a sheet and say: Well, here is Red Deer; it is bad

Supply

Veterans Affairs compared with the rest of Canada. I am not using that word myself; it is in the evidence. It makes it seem as though it is bad. Do not just simply say: Well, times are good in the country. The picture is reasonably good as far as V.L.A. settlers are concerned, but there is this dark spot in the Red Deer area.
I suggest to V.L.A. here that they make a very close examination of the things that happen in a local area before undertaking, as part of their general over-all policy, to put on the pressure during so-called good years.
Let it not be thought, Mr. Chairman, that I am offering one word of defence for the fellow who can pay and will not. I dare say there are some of those even in my own area, but I also dare say that they constitute a very small percentage of the total. I am not standing in defence of those persons. My associations with the V.L.A. boys in the Red Deer area have been what could be described as excellent. They have good men in there. They know conditions. They are trying to do their job well. I only hope that Ottawa, as I said before, will not just simply pick out one sheet after another and say the situation out there is bad; we have to get these boys in Red Deer to put the pressure on. Let them find out why there should be substantial arrears in that area.
I do not believe it is any criticism of V.L.A. at all. I come forth in defence actually in defence of my own area which, as I said at the beginning, is one of the finest mixed farming sections in the Dominion of Canada.
I thought probably that anyone reading this evidence might carry away an improper impression and certainly I feel it is my duty, knowing the facts, to make sure that no such incorrect impression is carried away by anyone.

This item provides for the payment of grants to veterans settled on provincial lands in accordance with agreements with provincial governments, and is reduced from $575,000 to $375,000, a reduction of $200,000. In view of the explanation given by the director to the committee that there had not been as many veterans taking advantage of this legislation as was expected,
I can understand the reduction; but I do hope the administration of the Veterans


Land Act does not throw up the sponge in this respect, because I am quite sure that as the years go by there will be more and more veterans settling under these terms. Up to recent years industrial conditions, wages and things of that sort have probably been against it. In addition to that, I do suggest that, particularly in the western provinces, that while we are supposed to have a great deal of land available for settlement it is remarkable how the land available for settlement close to roads and transportation is growing less and less each year. I do hope that the administration makes every effort to co-operate with any provincial government that has land available to try to get them to reserve suitable locations that may be used within the next few years.

This is the item that the hon. member for Battle River always took an intense interest in. It will be recalled that every year he had his annual resolution calling for free title for veterans. I am a little bit concerned to notice this year that the amount of the vote has been reduced from $150,000 to $25,000. I hope that means that now all those soldier settlers have had their outstanding liabilities reduced to an amount which is easily manageable on their part. I hate to hold the committee up, but I should like the assurance from the minister that now all those veterans still settled under the old Soldier Settlement Act have had their liabilities reduced. How many are left?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Without going into great detail in this matter, I might recall that the last time I made a statement on this question of reduction on soldier settlement debts was on January 27 of this year. At that time, following the speech of the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose, I brought down the number of cases remaining to 134 and that figure has now been reduced to 51, details of which are as follows. Twenty-two eligible contract holders wish to pay off their loan in accordance with their contract; 17 eligible contract holders do not qualify under the provisions of the order in council, that is their circumstances are such that a reduction is not warranted; 12

Supply
settlers are eligible and qualify for the reduction but notwithstanding repeated efforts on our part to have them make an acceptable offer they have for various reasons failed to do so. That makes 29 cases remaining to be dealt with. At that time I stated to the hon. member for Battle River -Camrose that I would personally go through the number of remaining files and I would be willing to discuss them with him. I have done so and after studying the record of these 29 cases I cannot help but think the director is right in his decision not to grant these 17 any reduction in debt in view of the circumstances in which they are now living.
Would $25,000 be adequate to reduce the debt?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Quite adequate.
